# Specialise Children Early by Motor Regime, Not by Sport: A Two-Stage Sport-School Model

**What it is** — The authors apply the convergence principle to youth: "particular consideration was given to the advisability of early specialisation, not in the specific type of sport, but in the specific motor regime involved" (Verkhoshansky 1963, 1972 cited). "orientation of the child to the sport and physical training with the sports means does not begin with specialised exercise to achieve competitive performance standards (which can easily lead to forced training). Instead, it begins with systematic management of the functional perfecting of the body" (PDF p. 306 / printed p. 295, checked against the page image). The model has two stages:
1. A child who shows "a predisposition to a particular form of athletic activity (e.g. quick reactions, speed of movement, a capacity for speed-strength activities or motor dexterity)" trains "in a group specialising in the appropriate motor regime (the first stage of a children's sport school in Russia)," using "a diversity of elementary motor forms which do not involve specialisation in some specific sport." "Competitions, primarily in team sports, are indispensable elements of such training because they involve those same elementary motor forms."
2. As demands rise, "the teacher will determine the child's predisposition to a specific sport and transfer him to the appropriate sport school for specialised training (the second stage)" (PDF p. 306 / printed p. 295).
The authors add that schools without this system can adopt it "if these two stages of early sporting preparation are applied systematically in a single school or club" (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296).

**Why it works** — The authors' reasons: specialising in a sport too early "can easily lead to forced training," and early training should raise "the body's functional abilities" through broad "elementary motor forms." In the convergence model, early specialisation "is firstly according to ability (but not to the physiological system) and is not related to the motor pattern" (PDF p. 306 / printed p. 295). They give no data for the model on these pages.

**When to apply** — Youth programmes and first-year college athletes with a narrow sport background: group by motor regime (speed, speed-strength, dexterity) and use varied elementary movements and team games before sport-specific loading. Eric's baseline: "Basic movement skills and basic lifts are taught before anything advanced, on the observed premise that many incoming athletes have high sport-specific skill from early specialization but poor general movement competency." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 173, Inferred, transcript). Inference: the authors' model is the upstream fix for the problem the baseline describes; at college age it can only be applied as remediation.

**When NOT to apply** — The basis is the authors' reference to Verkhoshansky's own 1963 and 1972 work and the Russian sport-school structure; no outcome data, ages or durations are given, hence `untested`. The model assumes a teacher can judge "predisposition" reliably, which the text does not test. Inference: Bompa's long-term sequential model in this library ([[periodization--bompa/framework--ltad-sequential-model]]) also delays sport specialisation (generally not before about 14-15 in most sports) and cites three longitudinal studies favouring a multilateral base; the two agree on direction. Bompa's model is multilateral rather than grouped by motor regime, so the authors' first-stage grouping by predisposition is their own addition. It does not address athletes who already specialised.

**Example** — The authors' own: a child showing quick reactions or a capacity for speed-strength activities joins a speed-strength motor-regime group at the first stage of a Russian children's sport school, then is transferred to a specific sport school at the second stage (PDF p. 306 / printed p. 295).

**Related** — [[principle--converging-partial-effects-of-strength-training-means]], [[claim--russian-sport-school-age-guidelines-table]], [[claim--heterochronicity-of-strength-quality-and-muscle-group-development-order]], [[periodization--bompa/framework--ltad-sequential-model]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--long-term-preparation-four-stage-model-and-directions]], [[block-periodization--issurin/heuristic--sensitive-periods-by-motor-ability-and-sex]]

"""Mechanical pre-promotion lint for Flint staged library folders.

Usage: python scripts/lint_library.py <book-folder> [<book-folder> ...]
Checks: body em dashes (header separators allowed), unresolved [[links]] (against staging
library + vault), review-history narration, confidence values, required sections.
"""
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

STAGING = Path("/Users/kristinarash/DEV/Flint/staging/library")
VAULT = Path("/Users/kristinarash/SecondBrain/Knowledge/library")
HEADER = re.compile(r"^\*\*[^*]+\*\* —")
HISTORY = re.compile(r"prior version|earlier draft|NO-GO|round[- ]1|round[- ]2|fix pass|fixer|this revision|previous version", re.I)
CONF = {"proven", "supported", "untested", "contested"}
SECTIONS = ["**What it is**", "**When NOT to apply**"]

known = set()
for root in (STAGING, VAULT):
    for p in root.rglob("*.md"):
        known.add(p.stem)
        known.add(p.relative_to(root).with_suffix("").as_posix())
        known.add(p.parent.name + "/" + p.stem)

problems = 0
for folder in sys.argv[1:]:
    for f in sorted(Path(folder).glob("*.md")):
        text = f.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        issues = []
        body_dash = [i + 1 for i, line in enumerate(text.splitlines())
                     if "—" in HEADER.sub("", line)]
        if body_dash:
            issues.append(f"body em dash lines {body_dash[:8]}")
        for link in re.findall(r"\[\[([^\]|#]+)", text):
            link = link.strip().removesuffix(".md")
            if link not in known and link.split("/")[-1] not in known:
                issues.append(f"unresolved [[{link}]]")
        if not f.name.startswith("_"):
            m = re.search(r"^confidence:\s*(\S+)", text, re.M)
            if not m or m.group(1).strip("\"'") not in CONF:
                issues.append(f"confidence={m.group(1) if m else 'missing'}")
            for s in SECTIONS:
                if s not in text:
                    issues.append(f"missing {s}")
            h = HISTORY.findall(text)
            if h:
                issues.append(f"review-history words {sorted(set(x.lower() for x in h))}")
        if issues:
            problems += len(issues)
            print(f"{f.parent.name}/{f.name}: " + "; ".join(issues))
print(f"TOTAL ISSUES: {problems}")

7	He maintains that progress in this regard will overcome the serious limitations imposed by simplistic 
8	application of classical principles of loading, especially that of progressive gradual overload. He considers that 
9	relevant scientific technology to monitor, analyse, offer biofeedback, refine and restore physical and mental 
10	functioning should play a major role in directing the training process, especially in enabling the athlete to cope with

12	that this type of applied sports science does not at all replace the entire concept of periodisation, but enriches ft to

14	Chronobiology and Periodisation
15	Future corroboration of the principles of periodisation may rely on some of the advances being made in the field of 
16	chronobiology which is examining the role played by biological clocks or pacemakers. Daily rhythms of structural 
17	and function change occur widely in biology, with most behavioral and physiological systems in mammals 
18	displaying at least some evidence of a 24 hour temporal structure. Although some of these daily rhythms may 
19	represent reactions to cyclic changes in light, temperature or other environmental stimuli, most reflect an innate 
20	timing program controlled by internal 24 hour biological clocks. The existence of such an endogenous 24 hour 
21	biological clock is the observation that daily rhythms of wakefulness and sleep can persist indefinitely in 
22	environments which exclude time cues such as natural light.
23	In such environments (e.g. underground caves), daily rhythms assume a regular periodicity that is 
24	approximately a day long (‘circadian’) rather than precisely 24 hours. Organisms, thus, have evolved mechanisms 
25	by which cyclic environmental stimuli can adjust the circadian clock each day to ensure that their rhythms remained 
26	synchronized to local time. The brain structures regulating the generation of rhythms and their entrainment by 
27	cyclic stimuli are collectively known as the ‘circadian system’.
28	Biological clocks provide at least two basic functions, namely awareness of local change (like a sundial) and 
29	measurement of the passage of time (like an hourglass). This allows the organism to maintain an internal temporal 
30	order and to anticipate change in order to enhance adaptation and survival. At the molecular level, a biological 
31	clock comprises a system of oscillating levels of proteins, controlled by transcription factors, which are proteins 
32	that switch specific genes on or off. In a scries of three papers. Young's group analysed the molecular workings of 
33	a major clock in drosophila flies, consisting of two proteins that initiate and control oscillation (Myers et al, 1995; 
34	Gekakis et al, 1995; Sehgal et al, 1995).
35	Since oscillatory processes lie at the heart of chronobiology, research is concentrating on how the endogenous 
36	oscillator works, how it synchronises with external cues and how time information is given by the oscillator to the 
37	rest of the cell, as well the overall interrelationship between environmental input, the oscillating mechanism, and 
38	the body’s response.
39	In 1972, scientists identified the brain's seat of circadian cycling in rats, the suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) 
40	(Moore & Eichler, 1972; Stephan & Zucker, 1972) and thereby narrowed down the search for the neural origins of 
41	the biological clock. The clock mechanism appears to reside in individual neurons in the SCN, but the mechanisms 
42	by which these neurons are coupled to form a stable oscillating ensemble have not yet been fully elucidated
43	From research to date, we then note that the circadian system in mammals comprises at least one master 
44	circadian pacemaker, a structure in the hypothalamus known as the suprachiasmatic nucleus that is entrained to the 
45	cycle of day and night by nervous input from the retina. Damage to this pacemaker disrupts or eliminates daily 
46	rhythms in animals. This pacemaker can also be shifted or entrained by other stimuli, such as an appropriately 
47	timed bouts of exercise, and certain hormones, neurotransmitters and drugs. The suprachiasmatic nucleus receives 
48	information from a limited number of brain structures, and these appear to be responsible for entraining the clock to 
49	periodic stimuli. The retinal input governs entrainment to the day-night cycle, whereas two other inputs (one from 
50	the thalamic intergeniculate structure, and another from the midbrain raphe nuclei) appear to play an important role 
51	in entraining or shifting rhythms by means of exercise and emotional arousal.
52	The possible link to periodisation of physical training then becomes apparent. Other pacemakers may also 
53	exist in mammals. For example, there is phenomenological evidence for a second pacemaker in humans that 
54	regulates the daily temperature cycle and other associated rhythms, although the interpretation of that data is 
55	contentious. The physical location of other possible pacemakers is unknown. There are numerous other texts which 
56	cover some of the advances in chronobiology and the nature of circadian rhythms, which are worthy of some study

64	6.4 Training as a Problem in M anagement
65	Programming and organisation of training require in-depth and comprehensive knowledge of the principles of 
66	training. It is appropriate, therefore, to examine programming as a problem in management.
67	The essence of management may be expressed in terms of the changcs of state of the relevant systems 
68	produced by given tasks, while the criterion of effectiveness lies in its functioning or development. Consequently, 
69	for practical implementation of management, it is necessary firstly to establish concepts about the structure of the 
70	managed system and the characteristics of raising it from one state to another.
71	Let us examine a logical scheme of training organisation for describing the components of management in 
72	sports training (Fig 6.12). Training is organised in accordance with specific tasks which result in a definite 
73	improvement in sports results, so that the degree of improvement in sporting performance is the criterion of the 
74	effectiveness of training. Sports results arc the observable product of the organisation of the athlete's external 
75	interactions. In other words, this is the result of the organisation of the athlete's movements which make effective 
76	use of strength and motor potential for executing specific motor tasks.
77	The patterning of the external influences and an increase in the relative contribution of those forces which 
78	directly contribute to the execution of the motor tasks are important conditions for improving sporting 
79	proficiency. Therefore, one has to identify the major components of management in sports training, as follows:
80	1. The complex of the athlete's external influences encountered in competition. The greater the athlete's motor 
81	potential, the more effectively the complex of external interactions can be organised. Therefore, in multi-year 
82	training, athletes train to increase their motor potential and specific work-capacity.
83	2. In this regard, the athlete's fitness state, as a characteristic of motor potential, should be classified as the 
84	second component of management in the system of sports training. In this context, fitness state refers to the 
85	athlete's structural-functional qualities which determine the athlete's potential to produce sporting prowess 
86	(Zatsiorsky, 1979). 
87	The complcx of external interactions and the athlete's fitness state are established 
88	effectively as a result of the systematic specialisation of the motor activities. The latter provides a number of 
89	specific training influences organised to produce the required changes in the complex comprising the external 
90	influences and the athlete's fitness state.
91	3. Consequently, specialised motor activities, i.e. the training load is the third component of management in the 
92	system of sport training (see 6.12).
93	Thus, the preceding components together represent an hierarchically organised complex which undergoes goal- 
94	directed changes during sports training. In training, the ordered influences address all three components of the 
95	management process simultaneously. However, the basis for changes of fitness state during training lies in a 
96	specific, cyclic sequence of events. The dosage of the training load is prescribed to promote changes in the 
97	athlete’s fitness state which, in turn, entails changcs in the complcx of external interactions of the athlete and a 
98	corresponding improvement in sporting results.
99	When the planned results are achieved, the programme and the organisation of the loading are determined 
100	for the next stage of training, and the sequence of the preceding conditions is repeated at higher levels. The 
101	cyclicity of this process in accordance with sport specific periodisation determines the contents of the athlete's 
102	training programme.
103	Completion of the tasks, executed as separate components of the complex system of management process, 
104	gives rise to an intricate dynamic complex of cause-effect relations between them, which may be considered as 
105	the structure of the managed system. Thus, the aggregate of the components of this complcx system, with its 
106	characteristic cause-cffcct connections, represents the overall managed system.
107	Thus, management involves all the tasks of training, motivation, the athlete's personality and social factors 
108	which express and integrate the interests of the athlete, coach and team, as well as the practical experience and 
109	theory of training construction. In orienting the course of training in a specific direction, model characteristics are 
110	quantitatively assigned which relate to the training load, the athlete’s fitness state and his external interactions 
111	(see Fig 6.12).

117	Figure 6.12 A logical scheme for organising sports training (Siff & Vcrkhoshansky, 1999).
118	The main idea of managing training consists of raising the fitness state of the body to a higher functional level. 
119	Control of this process is accomplished by assessing the effect at primarily two levels of management, namely at 
120	the level of the athlete's fitness state (control of the effect of the loading on fitness) and at the level of external 
121	interactions of the athlete (control of the change in their characteristics as a result of changes in fitness). Based on 
122	a comparison of different effects achieved at the levels indicated by the given model characteristics* suitable 
123	solutions are implemented in order to manage the later course of training. 
124	Analysis of the contents and 
125	organisation of training may now be summarised as follows:
126	1. Firstly, the interaction between the components of the managed system is determined by the training 
127	potential and the training effect of the loading (Fig 6.12). Here, the training potential o f the loading is 
128	understood to mean its potential for promoting adaptation of the body and corresponding changes in its 
129	fitness state and, consequently, in its external interactions. The training potential of the loading is a relative 
130	concept which should be examined and assessed in accordance with the athlete's current fitness state. 
131	Assessment o f the training effect of the loading means measuring the performance change that the loading 
132	produces in each case under competitive and laboratory conditions.
133	The training effect is achieved with relatively stable adaptation within the body, by use of any logical 
134	training programme. The basis for the training effect is the accumulation of adaptive traces within the body 
135	produced by the entire complex of training influences. The substantive meaning of training, encompassing 
136	the concepts of training potential and training effect of the loading has central significance for programming 
137	training and will be examined later in more detail.
138	2. The connection between the beginning and end points of training management is highly complex. The 
139	extent of this connection is determined primarily by the effectiveness of the operations of two 
140	interdependent subsystems of regulation (see Fig 6.12): {Training Load - Training Potential o f Loading - 
141	Athlete's Fitness State} (subsystem A) and {Training Effect o f Loading - Athlete's Fitness State • Athlete's 
142	External Interactions} (subsystem B). Assessment of the predictive reliability and the probability of success 
143	of regulation at the level of each subsystem shows one can be certain that the lower the measures for the first 
144	one (A), the weaker the link in the entire management system.
145	3. The necessity for effective management arises when there is a problem in selecting a training regime. In such 
146	situations success depends on the degree of accuracy in choosing the optimal from the multitude of possible 
147	solutions.

153	6.5 Prerequisites for Organising Training
154	A successful solution to the problem of programming and organising training cannot be obtained only by 
155	assembling the results of individual fragments of research. Intensive research is required to formulate usable 
156	concepts concerning the training process and identifying those conditions which determine its efficieni 
157	development. A preliminary examination of this problem already enables one to determine the goal of the task, 
158	the fundamental direction of research, and the specific information required (Fig 6.13).
159	The scheme need not be described in much detail, because its meaning and contents are sufficiently clear and 
160	their analysis is a matter for later discussion. Formulating a generalised theory of training requires a complcx 
161	approach to the organisation of research, without repeating those experimental errors which were proliferated 
162	during the preceding few decades.
163	Figure 6.13 A general theory of structuring sports training (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999).
164	In sport physiology especially, a divergence of the professional interests of specialists leads to the human body 
165	being regarded as two fairly distinct systems. Some specialists limit their study primarily to the neuromuscular 
166	system and its regulation by the CNS, applying their work largely to specd-strength and complex-technical types 
167	of sport. Others focus their interest on the cardiovascular-respiratory systems and metabolic processes which 
168	determine success in primarily cyclic types of sport.
169	Such specialisation is quite convenient for science, but is effective and applicable only on the basis of close 
170	integration between theory and practice. All too often, studies are based on the effect of a single factor on 
171	performance; very rarely does research focus on the interactive effects of concurrent or sequential complexes of 
172	training methods.
173	338
174	
175

177	SUPERTRAINING
178	In particular, understanding of the scientific and practical fundamentals of the development of general 
179	endurance suffers. Attention is centred on the mechanism of energy production, which ignores the specialisation 
180	of the muscular apparatus as the direct executor of work, and general endurance is considered exclusively to be a 
181	(unction of respiratory potential. Therefore, physiologists were perplexed when information was revealed about 
182	the decrease in V02max during the competition period and the unexpectedly low V02max levels among many 
183	athletes in cyclic sports. However, this should not have been unexpected if they had concurrently examined the 
184	contractile and metabolic characteristics of the muscles of athletes who specialise in general endurance sports.
185	Sport training theory also abounds with misdirected efforts. Here there is a similar division in the interests of 
186	specialists who give preference primarily to speed-strength or cyclic sports and tend to minimise the role of 
187	general endurance training. This professional specialisation cannot be condemned if they limit their theoretical 
188	and practical generalisations to 'their' types of sport. It is when they attempt to apply the same principles and 
189	methods to other types of sport that this single-minded approach becomes misleading.
190	A definite weakness in modem sports training theory is the result of underestimating the importance of 
191	information obtained from physiological and biochemical research in sport, as well as from the limited amount of 
192	definitive scientific information which forms the basis for establishing training principles. 
193	Until recently, 
194	generalised practical experience was usually regarded as the only valid way of establishing effective training 
195	principles and methods, thereby neglecting the important contributions of scientific research. At the same time, 
196	scientists disdained this attitude and coaches regarded scientists as impractical theoreticians, with the result that 
197	their individual bodies of information were not shared and training methodology suffered. The advancement of 
198	sport now depends strongly on close cooperation between scientists, coaches and athletes.
199	6.6 Basic M anagem ent Theory
200	In most interactions in the work, social or recreational setting, leaders or managers emerge or are appointed to 
201	control, coordinate and guide their fellow humans to carry out certain tasks or achieve specific goals or fulfill a 
202	prescribed purpose.
203	The terms leadership and management are often used interchangeably, but there are distinct differences 
204	between the two, depending on the situation. Small, ephemeral groups may have leaders or elected chairpersons, 
205	but usually not managers. The chairman of the board of a company does not play the managerial role of the 
206	executive director, who in turn does not function like the sales manager, who also may act as the highly motivating 
207	leader of a sales team. Sports teams have captains, who are special types of leader, but they also have managers 
208	who have no leadership function whatsoever on the field of play. Similarly, captains usually have no prescribed 
209	leadership role off the field. Military officers often have to fill roles of leadership and management. What is 
210	common to both leadership and management is the task of marshalling together the abilities and efforts of groups of 
211	individuals to reach specific goals, whether social, economic, military, sporting or otherwise. What is also common 
212	to both is that communication is essential to the entire process.
213	Tellier states that management roles are determined by position in an organisation and are characterised by 
214	three basic elements: responsibility, authority and accountability. Leadership, on the other hand, implies power to 
215	influence others, which relies on factors such as expertise, personality and charisma.
216	Management and leadership both require an understanding of human behaviour in terms of needs, wants and 
217	drives, hence the next section introduces you to theories of human behaviour and motivation.
218	6.6.1 Human Needs and Motivation
219	Although many models have been formulated to explain human needs, only a few have been selected here to enable 
220	you to appreciate the strengths and weaknesses of each and be able to select a suitable model for a given situation 
221	(Siff, 1990). The motivation process involved in human drive may be summarized in the following way (Fig 6.14):

227	At this point it is relevant to discuss the relationship between performance and motivation or. arousal. Higher levdr 
228	of arousal do not necessarily lead to increased performance, on the contrary, excessive arousal may lead to a drop a 
229	performance, lowered productivity and an increase in the incidencc of mistakes and accidents. There appears to be 
230	an optimum level of arousal for any person performing a specific task at a specific time, as was revealed by the 
231	work of Yerkes and Dodson (see Fig 6.15).
232	The exact shape of the curve depends on individual characteristics such as level of introversion/extroversion, 
233	level of exhaustion, standard of health, and task complexity. There is no easy formula to determine the 
234	characteristic curve for any individual; instead it depends on the effort of a manager, leader or coach to become 
235	adequately informed of the personal attributes, performance and characteristics of each worker or athlete. What is 
236	relevant is that the manager or coach appreciates that all motivational techniques are not universally applicable to 
237	everyone. Instead, they are to be applied with a thorough understanding of the individual and the situation.
238	Caution must be exercised when applying the Yerkes-Dodson (Y-D) model, since it implies that there is just 
239	one discrete peak for a specific optimal level of arousal or stress. The existence of the 'second wind' phenomenon 
240	(curve B) and the effect of task complexity on curve shape are two of several reasons why the original curve must 
241	be applied to restoration and stress management with circumspection.
242	It also implies that very low and very high levels of arousal invariably lead to diminished performance. While 
243	this may be generally true, it is well known that both sensory underload and overload may lead to phases of 
244	enhanced performance (curves A, C). The consequences of low arousal levels is not necessarily sleep or coma. On 
245	the contrary, meditation and similar altered states of consciousness may enhance performance in certain situations 
246	(curve A).
247	Moreover, sleep, reverie, day-dreaming and relaxed visualisation should not be viewed always as unproductive 
248	and disconnected, since research and experience reveal that problem-solving, creativity and physiological repair 
249	may occur strongly in these altered, though perfectly normal, states. The occurrence of nightmares and vigorous 
250	muscular activity also suggests that high stress levels may persist even in sleep.
251	Notions of optimising one's stress level thus may be seen to be based on a limited mechanistic model of human 
252	behaviour. Altered states of consciousness are a normal part of life and are not adequately described by the Y-D or 
253	Selye curves. In fact, the most efficient use and channeling of 'stress energy' may be mediated during periodic 
254	altered states which the Y-D model describes as inadequately stressful to produce meaningful performance (cunt 
255	A). Therefore, both optimisation and transcendental stress management strategies are necessary if effective use is to 
256	be made of stress.
257	Furthermore, regular exposure to a stressor may produce either habituation or oversensitisation, so that the 
258	same level of stress may not produce the same response at a later stage. In either event, timely use of restoration 
259	measures is of central importance.
260	Personality can have a significant effect on the shape of the Y-D curve. For instance, the introvert appears to 
261	have a lower optimal arousal zone, unlike the extrovert who requires greater stimulation and can cope better with 
262	high levels of stress. This difference in the effect of high levels of training and competitive stress has important 
263	implications for the prescription of restorative procedures, with the introvert probably requiring early restoration 
264	and the extrovert requiring careful monitoring to prevent overtraining caused by a desire for greater stimulation.
265	Task structure also modifies the shape of the Y-D curve. Complex tasks require low levels of arousal to reach 
266	optimal performance over very limited periods (e.g. in golf, gymnastics and pole vaulting), whereas simple sports 
267	tasks may be executed over a longer period at higher levels of arousal.

274	Other Theories of Needs
275	Aldcrfer identified the following categories of needs:
276	• Existence needs, which concern our physiological and material desires, such as those for hunger and shelter
277	• Relatedness needs, which concern relationships between people
278	• Growth needs, which concern personal development, change, evolution and creativity.
279	McClelland, like the neurophysiologist, James Olds, however, maintained that there arc only two human needs ~ 
280	the need for pleasure and the need to avoid pain. All other needs or motives are learned. On this basis, McClelland 
281	then categorized these acquired needs as follows:
282	• Achievement. There is a strong need among some people to excel. They have a high achievement need and 
283	want to do a task well for its own sake, rather than for its material rewards.
284	• Power. This refers to the desire to influence, regulate and control the actions and behaviour of other people.
285	• Affiliation This refers to the need for positive relationships with other people and probably is described best 
286	by the word 'friendship’. A major aspect of the affiliation need is the need for communication.
287	Alderfer’s model differs significantly from Maslow's in that it recognizes that satisfied needs may still continue to 
288	be influential, particularly if they can substitute for an unsatisfied need. Research by Alderfer also reveals that 
289	higher order (growth) needs can arise or exist simultaneously with the lower order needs. It also emerges that 
290	certain needs become even more intensified if they are more satisfied than others. It is obvious then that Maslow's 
291	hierarchy, like all theory, has to be applied with circumspection.
292	341
293	complex training tasks can lead rapidly to ‘overstrcss*, while simple tasks may be insufficiently challenging to 
294	produce continued supercompensation. A balance between complexity, simplicity, intensity and volume of load is 
295	necessary to ensure growth and to minimise overtraining.
296	Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs
297	One of the best known, though simplistic, models of human needs is that of psychologist, Abraham Maslow. He 
298	devised an hierarchy of needs ranging from the most basic, which have to be satisfied first before subsequent 
299	needs will begin to exert a significant influence on a person. This hierarchy may be arranged in the form of a 
300	triangle with the most basic physiological, concrete needs at its base and the highest level, abstract need for 
301	self-actualization (the need to achieve one's highest potential in a specific situation) at its apex. It may also be 
302	arranged to explain the needs of the individual in both a private or a professional capacity (see Fig 6.16).
303	Occasionally, this model may include a state beyond self-actualisation, called transcendence which is 
304	associated with states of profoundly altered consciousness such as religious reverie or trance meditation. 
305	However, this state is not simply the preserve of the ascetic or mystic, because many athletes have reported 
306	achieving world class performances in similar altered states (Murphy & White, 1978)
307

311	All the above theories overlap in some respects or have strong similarities. They are usefully augmented or 
312	replaced in the analysis of management interactions by Vroom's Expectancy Theory o f Motivation, which can b: 
313	particularly valuable to apply in the workplace or advertising realm. This theory posits that it is not merely i 
314	specific goal, but the individual perception of that goal which motivates people. Vroom stated that Motivate 
315	Force depends on two factors (Tellier, 1978):
316	• the perceived attractiveness (valence V) of the goal or outcome
317	• the perceived probability o f achieving that goal or outcome (one's personal belief, B, that success is likely)
318	He then combined these two factors so that the Motivational Force F depends on their arithmetic product F = V X
319	B. 
320	In other words, if a goal is highly attractive and you believe strongly that it is within your reach, tht 
321	Motivational Force driving you will be very strong. However, if a goal is extremely attractive, but you believe it to 
322	be far outside your reach, you will experience a small Motivational Force and put in minimal effort to attain that 
323	goal. Under such circumstances, it is desirable to break down a large or distant goal into smaller goals to be 
324	achieved over a period or at a rate which you perceive to be more matched to your capabilities or experience.
325	Vroom's detailed theory involves allocating numerical values to the contributing factors. Perceived 
326	attractiveness is rated from -5 (extremely undesirable) to +5 (extremely desirable), while belief in success is rated 
327	on a scale from 0 (total disbelief) to 1 (total belief)- The overall Motivational Force is the sum of the motivational 
328	forces calculated from the products of perceived attractiveness and perceived belief for all the important goals or 
329	outcomes associated with carrying out the task.
330	Detailed examples of this theory are outside the scope of this book, so it is sufficient to note that a manager or 
331	leader can motivate athletes strongly if he appreciates that motivation depends on perceptions of goal attractiveness 
332	and attainability. He can improve performance either by modifying the task accordingly or by altering the athlete’s 
333	perceptions of the task and its outcomes.
334	6.6.2 Management Models
335	Management implies the existence of authority. Oncken identifies four types of authority: authority of position or 
336	power, authority of personality, authority of competence, and authority of integrity.
337	The Traditional Model
338	Tradition decreed that workers were of secondary importance to productivity, that they were possessions, slaves or 
339	hired slaves. This linear approach to management may be summarized in the form of the following diagram (Fig 
340	6.17). All too often this model continues to be applied by managers, leaders and coaches steeped in the traditional
341	ways.
342	E xpectancy Theory of M otivation
343	Figure 6.17 The linear, single continuum model of traditional management
344	The Managerial Grid
345	Experience and subsequent research have revealed that productivity is enhanced if an appropriate balance is 
346	established between concern for people and production. This led Blake and Mouton to devise the Ohio State 
347	University model, which emphasizes the relationship between productivity and people concern (Fig 6.18).
348	All management styles may be identified by selecting suitable coordinates from the grid. For instance, the 
349	autocrat would have a rating of (9,1), whereas the laissez faire leader would have a rating of (1,9). Coordinates 
350	(1,1) characterize impoverished leadership, while (9,9) refers to ideal management. The middle-of-the-road 
351	manager is located at (5,5).

358	Situational Leadership
359	Hcrscy and Blanchard stated that leadership style ought to be implemented according to each situation which arises. 
360	Their model illustrates how leadership style may be adapted to a given situation according to the ’maturity' 
361	(education, experience, responsibility, self-motivation, degree of self-actualization) of the worker or follower (Fig 
362	6.19).
363	Figure 6.19 The Situational Leadership Model (Hersey and Blanchard)
364	To use this system, the coach in playing a role as leader rates the maturity of the follower as low, moderate or high 
365	(Ml, M2, M3 or M4), then reads off the appropriate leadership style (SI, S2, S3 or S4) in the relevant box above. 
366	Relationship behaviour includes the amount of time and effort put into interaction with followers. One spends more 
367	time in Selling or Participatory situations than in Telling or Delegating situations, hence the shape of the curve.
368	The Leadership Continuum
369	Tannenbaum and Schmidt devised a leadership continuum extending between the extremes of Leader-ccntredness 
370	and Worker-centredness. It relates well to the leadership characteristics of Likert’s four management styles, as 
371	follows (Fig 6.20).

378	Decision Making and Problem Solving
379	Decision-making is a vital part of all management situations, so it is essential that some of the formal theory of this 
380	process be covered. Often, managers or committees are called upon to handle problems in order of importance. The 
381	word 'Importance' is far too unspecific to be of any real value in every situation; it is relative to the individual 
382	perceptions of all concerned in the problem solving or decision-making process. It is preferable to rate every 
383	problem in terms of:
384	• Seriousness or size
385	• Urgency
386	• Growth potential or growth rate
387	In using such a system, one allocates H (high), M (medium) or L (low) to each of these factors relating to all the 
388	problems to be considered in a particular situation. Problems identified by triple or double H’s are then handled 
389	before those with fewer or no H's, with triple L's rated problems receiving lowest priority. In attempting to solve 
390	any problem, it is useful to recognize the main six steps in problem-solving:
391	1. Identification and definition of problem
392	2. Generation of alternative solutions
393	3. Evaluation of the alternative solutions
394	4. Decision -making: selection of solution
395	5. Implementation of decision
396	6. Testing of solution.
397	Should the final step verify the value of the chosen solution, the process will terminate. If not, one may return to

425	6.7 Classification of Sports
426	Establishing the principles and rules of programming training necessitates determining clearly the limits of 
427	generality and specificity in individual sports or groups of related sports. To do this it is necessary to classify 
428	sports scientifically to establish programming criteria.
429	Sport is associated first of all, with the spatio-temporal organisation of the athlete's movements, which is 
430	determined by the rules and conditions of competition and by the effective use of motor potential for executing 
431	the required motor tasks. 
432	In all cases, this requires perfecting the central nervous processes which control 
433	movement, as well as raising the functional potential of the muscles and metabolic systems. Classification of 
434	sports into individual, team, ball or water sports, for example, is not scientifically useful; it is more appropriate to 
435	classify sports on the basis of the particular organisation of the sporting movements and characteristics of the 
436	physical systems used to produce their working effect.
437	The more prolonged and the lower the intensity of muscular work, the greater the role of aerobic processes 
438	and the greater the functional specialisation of the muscles to utilise oxygen more fully. 
439	The role o f the 
440	glycolytic mechanisms of energy production grows as the duration of work decreases and the power of muscular 
441	work increases. The muscles adapt to working conditions of an inadequate supply of oxygen and the rapid 
442	removal of lactate during the exercise.
443	The loading of the motor apparatus and the power of explosive effort increase significantly during brief 
444	acyclic work. Under conditions of heavy dynamic overload, athletes must overcome significant external 
445	resistance which they must accomplish in a very short time (tenths and even hundredths of a second). This 
446	complicates movement coordination significantly and requires the development of an effective and reliable 
447	biodynamic structure (see 2.1.3). Under these conditions, the neuromuscular apparatus improves intramuscular 
448	regulation and increases the power of anaerobic energy production. This preamble shows that sports may be 
449	divided into two broad groups, namely acyclic and cyclic sports:

455	• Acyclic sports characterised by the complex organisation of motor actions and an intense concentration of 
456	working effort, displayed briefly under competition conditions. Such sports have an inherently stable 
457	biodynamic movement structure and defmite structural-functional specialisation of the neuromuscular 
458	apparatus which recruits its abilities to display powerful explosive effort and anaerobic power; primarily 
459	through ATP-CP energy processes.
460	• Cyclic sports characterised by prolonged repetition of stereotyped work cycles of relatively simple 
461	organisation which do not require maximal muscular tension. The energy acquired for such work comes 
462	primarily from stored glycogen or free fatty acids metabolised in the presence of oxygen during the exercise. 
463	One of the most important conditions for improving performance in this group of sports is the structural and 
464	functional specialisation of the muscles to improve their ability to oxidise metabolites, as well as to increase 
465	the capacity of the metabolic processes and the economy of using the energy substrates during exercise.
466	One should further subdivide the sports in each of these broad groups in terms of specific characteristics of 
467	movement organisation and energy production. Thus, the acyclic group embraces sports that require powerful, 
468	brief, explosive efforts and others which involve fine motor control and spatially precise movement. In the 
469	cyclical group there are some sports where the work is executed under conditions of extensive oxygen utilisation 
470	and others where the muscles have an inadequate oxygen supply.
471	Finally, one should identify a third group of sports, characterised by varying competition demands and the 
472	need to maintain a high work output under conditions of fatigue. These types of sports combine characteristics of 
473	the preceding two groups. They involve constant changes in intensity of the competition activities, as well as 
474	bursts of high power movements with periodic rest pauses, so that energy production is of a mixed aerobic- 
475	anaerobic character, with the greater part being derived from glycolytic reactions. Thus we may classify sports 
476	into three groups, as already outlined by Farfel (1969):
477	• Acyclic sports, in which perfecting of the neuromuscular system for precise regulation of movements and the 
478	ability to produce great power play the dominant roles
479	• Cyclic sports (usually of submaximal and of moderate power), associated primarily with the production of 
480	muscular work through aerobic processes
481	• Complex (combined) sports, where characteristically there is a high variability of motor actions under 
482	conditions of advancing fatigue and varying intensity of work, typified by team sports and one-on-one events 
483	(e.g. boxing and fencing).
484	In classifying sports, it is necessary to consider competitive, as well as training activities. This is important, 
485	because in some cases the training exercises are very different from competitive actions, often due to the 
486	necessity for repeated reproduction of the competitive movements in training. In practice, we refer to special 
487	endurance (e.g. speed-jumping-, and strength-endurance) in such cases. For example, the shortest sprint distance 
488	in track-and-field (100 metres) is covered in approximately 10 seconds. The effort expended to achieve this does 
489	not depend on oxidative efficiency. However, in order for a sprinter to prepare himself to effectively display such 
490	effort, he should execute training loads that develop his aerobic and anaerobic potential, in particular the latter. 
491	The general principles of programming training for each of the above groups of sport will be examined later.

496	characteristics of the structural and functional specialisation of the body as a specific external expression of long­
497	term adaptation to intense muscular work. Finally, we will investigate some of the characteristics of developing 
498	technical proficiency in different sports to understand how the athlete masters the skill to use motor potential 
499	efficiently in competition.

502	brief training stimuli in sport (the immediate training effect). It has been shown that the after-effect of large 
503	loading docs not simply restore the expended energy but leads to super-restoration which exceeds the initial level

523	obey common sense, which indicates that the fundamental unit of training should be the mesocycle and not the

575	heterochronicity is determined by:
576	• the action of particular physiological systems in establishing long-term adaptation of a specific emphasis

693	6.8.2 Structural-Functional Specialisation in Training
694	Structural-functional specialisation refers to those stable, adaptive changes that are produced by the specific form 
695	of conditioning imposed by a given sport. 
696	All of the survival systems of the body undergo adaptive 
697	reconstruction in response to external stressors. However, it is not difficult to observe that those systems which 
698	are of major importance for success in sport undergo an accelerated rate of functional growth.
699	350
700	
701	
702	######## PDF 362 (printed 351) imgs=2 draws=0
703	SUPERTRAINING
704	It has been noted already that the specifics of adaptation are determined primarily by two factors, namely the 
705	work regime in sports, and the gradual, but steady increase in complexity of the body's external interactions 
706	associated with the growth of sporting proficiency.
707	For example, improvement of the triple jump requires developing the ability of the motor apparatus to 
708	produce great power. Increase in jumping distance, which is accomplished primarily by increasing running 
709	speed, is associated with a significant increase in complexity of the interaction of the feet with the support at each 
710	take-off, a situation that requires significant improvement in reactive ability.
711	Cyclic locomotion, to a great extent, necessitates increasing the power and the capacity of the body's systems 
712	which are crucial for energy production of muscular work. Energy expenditure increases greatly with increase in 
713	movement speed. For example, oxygen requirements increase considerably with running speed, energy 
714	expenditure being almost proportional to the fourth power of running speed (Sargent, 1926). This rising cost of 
715	running speed is associated with a greater reliance being placed on anaerobic processes for generating the 
716	necessary energy of work (Henry, 1951; Margaria, 1963).
717	As discussed previously (see 2.2.3, 5.4.3). two forms of functional perfecting of the body may be 
718	distinguished in the training process, namely, specialisation by physiological system and specialisation by motor 
719	ability (Verkhoshansky, 1971). The most obvious evidence of specialisation appears when comparing the 
720	functional development of the body in different sports. 
721	If we refer to the classification scheme of 6.5, 
722	specialisation by physiological system means that acyclic sports rely predominantly on anaerobic processes and 
723	functional hypertrophy of the motor apparatus, whereas cyclic sports place major reliance on aerobic processes. 
724	In complex (combined) sports, there is an intense functional development of both the motor apparatus and the 
725	energy production systems. 
726	Specialisation by motor ability refers to the exact programme of neuromuscular 
727	control that is developed by repetitive execution of the motor skills required in a given sport (see 2.2.3).
728	However, it is important to emphasize that specialisation in the first two cases does not imply that 
729	development is either strictly aerobic or anaerobic, but rather that there is a particular primary emphasis of 
730	functional specialisation. One can successfully develop a high level of explosive strength in acyclic locomotion 
731	only when one possesses sufficiently high aerobic efficiency. At the same time, improving the efficiency of the 
732	energy producing systems in cyclic locomotion should be based on highly developed muscular strength and local 
733	muscular endurance.
734	The kinesiological patterns of motor activity in various types of sports are approximately equivalent, 
735	although there are some qualitative and quantitative differences associated with specific types of sports. Thus, 
736	sprint swimmers have higher rates and developmental levels of anaerobic productivity than distance swimmers, 
737	whereas aerobic productivity is superior for distance swimmers. This is determined by the emphasis of the 
738	training.
739	In the multi-year training of sprinters, up to Class I-CMS (Class I - Candidate for Master of Sport), the chief 
740	emphasis is on developing general (aerobic) endurance and speed, whereas at MS-MSIC (Master of Sport - 
741	Master of Sport, International Class) level the emphasis is on developing speed (anaerobic) endurance. In the 
742	training of distance athletes of all qualification levels, the chief emphasis is on developing aerobic productivity, 
743	while at the MS-MSIC level, the emphasis is on enhancing anaerobic productivity (Vankov, 1978).
744	In cyclic sports, strength preparedness, mainly in the form of strcngth-endurancc, plays an important role. 
745	Research shows that, with a relatively moderate increase in muscular strength, together with a rise in the athlete's 
746	qualification, the qualities of dynamic strength-endurance and power accelerate the increase in functional strength 
747	(Zhurbinoi, 1978).
748	The process of functional specialisation is characterised by the fact that there is a definite sequence (known 
749	as hcterochronicity, as detailed in 2.2.3) in the development of adaptation. This means that the body adapts to 
750	external influences only when they bccome necessary for the further growth of sporting proficiency, and this 
751	involves only those systems whose functions satisfy all the necessary requirements for enhancing sport specific 
752	fitness.
753	The multi-year functional specialisation of the body is closely connected with its corresponding physical 
754	adaptation. This adaptation leaves traces of the training influences on the body for long periods and serves as the 
755	foundation for its functional perfecting. These traces have been studied extensively in general terms at the level of 
756	muscle tissue, cardiac muscle, skeletal structure, cardiovascular mechanisms and other systems. Further study of 
757	the multi-year characteristics of structural-functional specialisation in particular types of sport is important in 
758	formulating the principles of programming training.

764	6.8.3 The Structure of Special Physical Preparedness
765	The above-mentioned characteristics of functional specialisation in multi-year training are associated with 
766	specific adaptive changes in the cardiovascular-respiratory and neuromuscular systems, as well as in the 
767	efficiency of the central nervous mechanisms that regulate their activities. For many years, it was not appreciated 
768	that each type of sport requires not only a distinct type of motor skill, but also a different type of physiological 
769	fitness. Even today, the role and nature of supplementary training is not clearly understood. For example, much 
770	the same sort of resistance training may be prescribed for many different athletes in various sports, simply 
771	because the sports seem to be superficially similar. 
772	It must be realised that supplementary or 'cross' training 
773	cannot simply be used in a very general way in the belief that strength, speed or endurance acquired in one 
774	situation will be of direct benefit to performance in another situation.
775	For example, muscle endurance gained through supplementary running training does not mean that it will 
776	directly improve the performance of a competitive rower or cyclist. Special physical preparedness (SPP) depends 
777	on developing the necessary physiological qualities with the same muscles and neuromuscular mechanisms that 
778	are encountered in the given sport. Therefore, training for special physical preparedness must be based on a 
779	thorough understanding of the different types of specificity discussed in 1.3 and the characteristics of the 
780	interaction between the various organs and the neuromuscular system, which determines the change in special 
781	work capacity.
782	It was also assumed that one could develop each fitness quality separately with some or other form of general 
783	training, then assemble all of them to produce the necessary sport specific fitness from them. The emergence of 
784	specificity from an array of non-specific fitness qualities, however, is not supported by current physiological and 
785	biochemical research, so it is clear that the management of training must take into consideration the effects of 
786	concurrent and sequential training means. Therefore, the problem of programming training was examined from 
787	several different positions in earlier chapters (see especially 3.2.1 regarding speed and quickness, and 4.4 
788	regarding general endurance).
789	6.9 Preparedness and the Training Load
790	The connection between the athlete's fitness state and a given loading regime is the central issue in the theory and 
791	practice of programming training (sec 6.3). It is also the weakest link in the management of training, which 
792	requires the special attention of scientists and coaches. Before examining the practical aspects of the connection 
793	between loading and the athlete's fitness state, the concepts of training load and training effect must be defined 
794	more thoroughly (see Fig 6.12).
795	Strictly speaking, the training load does not exist as an independent entity. Terminologically, it must be 
796	distinguished from the load used in weight training, which refers to the resistance or force imposed on the body 
797	by a weight or machinc. Training load is related to the muscular work which the body must produce to carry out 
798	a given regime of exercise in training or competition. More precisely, muscular work is that training potential 
799	which elicits an appropriate training effect from the body. Thus, the training potential of muscular work, and 
800	consequently its training effect is to a large extent determined by the athlete’s current fitness state.
801	It should be clear that the interrelation between the athlete's fitness state and the training load is extremely 
802	complex, dependent upon many factors and determined by numerous variables (see Fig 6.12). Unfortunately, 
803	research concerning this connection is limited and often contradictory. 
804	Therefore, this chapter attempts to 
805	systematise and examine the connection between the athlete's fitness state and the training load, drawing largely 
806	upon the results of extensive research by Verkhoshansky and his co-workers.
807	6.9.1 The Training Load and its Effect

He maintains that progress in this regard will overcome the serious limitations imposed by simplistic 
application of classical principles of loading, especially that of progressive gradual overload. He considers that 
relevant scientific technology to monitor, analyse, offer biofeedback, refine and restore physical and mental 
functioning should play a major role in directing the training process, especially in enabling the athlete to cope with

Chronobiology and Periodisation
Future corroboration of the principles of periodisation may rely on some of the advances being made in the field of 
chronobiology which is examining the role played by biological clocks or pacemakers. Daily rhythms of structural 
and function change occur widely in biology, with most behavioral and physiological systems in mammals 
displaying at least some evidence of a 24 hour temporal structure. Although some of these daily rhythms may 
represent reactions to cyclic changes in light, temperature or other environmental stimuli, most reflect an innate 
timing program controlled by internal 24 hour biological clocks. The existence of such an endogenous 24 hour 
biological clock is the observation that daily rhythms of wakefulness and sleep can persist indefinitely in 
environments which exclude time cues such as natural light.
In such environments (e.g. underground caves), daily rhythms assume a regular periodicity that is 
approximately a day long (‘circadian’) rather than precisely 24 hours. Organisms, thus, have evolved mechanisms 
by which cyclic environmental stimuli can adjust the circadian clock each day to ensure that their rhythms remained 
synchronized to local time. The brain structures regulating the generation of rhythms and their entrainment by 
cyclic stimuli are collectively known as the ‘circadian system’.
Biological clocks provide at least two basic functions, namely awareness of local change (like a sundial) and 
measurement of the passage of time (like an hourglass). This allows the organism to maintain an internal temporal 
order and to anticipate change in order to enhance adaptation and survival. At the molecular level, a biological 
clock comprises a system of oscillating levels of proteins, controlled by transcription factors, which are proteins 
that switch specific genes on or off. In a scries of three papers. Young's group analysed the molecular workings of 
a major clock in drosophila flies, consisting of two proteins that initiate and control oscillation (Myers et al, 1995; 
Gekakis et al, 1995; Sehgal et al, 1995).
Since oscillatory processes lie at the heart of chronobiology, research is concentrating on how the endogenous 
oscillator works, how it synchronises with external cues and how time information is given by the oscillator to the 
rest of the cell, as well the overall interrelationship between environmental input, the oscillating mechanism, and 
the body’s response.
In 1972, scientists identified the brain's seat of circadian cycling in rats, the suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) 
(Moore & Eichler, 1972; Stephan & Zucker, 1972) and thereby narrowed down the search for the neural origins of 
the biological clock. The clock mechanism appears to reside in individual neurons in the SCN, but the mechanisms 
by which these neurons are coupled to form a stable oscillating ensemble have not yet been fully elucidated
From research to date, we then note that the circadian system in mammals comprises at least one master 
circadian pacemaker, a structure in the hypothalamus known as the suprachiasmatic nucleus that is entrained to the 
cycle of day and night by nervous input from the retina. Damage to this pacemaker disrupts or eliminates daily 
rhythms in animals. This pacemaker can also be shifted or entrained by other stimuli, such as an appropriately 
timed bouts of exercise, and certain hormones, neurotransmitters and drugs. The suprachiasmatic nucleus receives 
information from a limited number of brain structures, and these appear to be responsible for entraining the clock to 
periodic stimuli. The retinal input governs entrainment to the day-night cycle, whereas two other inputs (one from 
the thalamic intergeniculate structure, and another from the midbrain raphe nuclei) appear to play an important role 
in entraining or shifting rhythms by means of exercise and emotional arousal.
The possible link to periodisation of physical training then becomes apparent. Other pacemakers may also 
exist in mammals. For example, there is phenomenological evidence for a second pacemaker in humans that 
regulates the daily temperature cycle and other associated rhythms, although the interpretation of that data is 
contentious. The physical location of other possible pacemakers is unknown. There are numerous other texts which 
cover some of the advances in chronobiology and the nature of circadian rhythms, which are worthy of some study

6.4 Training as a Problem in M anagement
Programming and organisation of training require in-depth and comprehensive knowledge of the principles of 
training. It is appropriate, therefore, to examine programming as a problem in management.
The essence of management may be expressed in terms of the changcs of state of the relevant systems 
produced by given tasks, while the criterion of effectiveness lies in its functioning or development. Consequently, 
for practical implementation of management, it is necessary firstly to establish concepts about the structure of the 
managed system and the characteristics of raising it from one state to another.
Let us examine a logical scheme of training organisation for describing the components of management in 
sports training (Fig 6.12). Training is organised in accordance with specific tasks which result in a definite 
improvement in sports results, so that the degree of improvement in sporting performance is the criterion of the 
effectiveness of training. Sports results arc the observable product of the organisation of the athlete's external 
interactions. In other words, this is the result of the organisation of the athlete's movements which make effective 
use of strength and motor potential for executing specific motor tasks.
The patterning of the external influences and an increase in the relative contribution of those forces which 
directly contribute to the execution of the motor tasks are important conditions for improving sporting 
proficiency. Therefore, one has to identify the major components of management in sports training, as follows:
1. The complex of the athlete's external influences encountered in competition. The greater the athlete's motor 
potential, the more effectively the complex of external interactions can be organised. Therefore, in multi-year 
training, athletes train to increase their motor potential and specific work-capacity.
2. In this regard, the athlete's fitness state, as a characteristic of motor potential, should be classified as the 
second component of management in the system of sports training. In this context, fitness state refers to the 
athlete's structural-functional qualities which determine the athlete's potential to produce sporting prowess 
(Zatsiorsky, 1979). 
The complcx of external interactions and the athlete's fitness state are established 
effectively as a result of the systematic specialisation of the motor activities. The latter provides a number of 
specific training influences organised to produce the required changes in the complex comprising the external 
influences and the athlete's fitness state.
3. Consequently, specialised motor activities, i.e. the training load is the third component of management in the 
system of sport training (see 6.12).
Thus, the preceding components together represent an hierarchically organised complex which undergoes goal- 
directed changes during sports training. In training, the ordered influences address all three components of the 
management process simultaneously. However, the basis for changes of fitness state during training lies in a 
specific, cyclic sequence of events. The dosage of the training load is prescribed to promote changes in the 
athlete’s fitness state which, in turn, entails changcs in the complcx of external interactions of the athlete and a 
corresponding improvement in sporting results.
When the planned results are achieved, the programme and the organisation of the loading are determined 
for the next stage of training, and the sequence of the preceding conditions is repeated at higher levels. The 
cyclicity of this process in accordance with sport specific periodisation determines the contents of the athlete's 
training programme.
Completion of the tasks, executed as separate components of the complex system of management process, 
gives rise to an intricate dynamic complex of cause-effect relations between them, which may be considered as 
the structure of the managed system. Thus, the aggregate of the components of this complcx system, with its 
characteristic cause-cffcct connections, represents the overall managed system.
Thus, management involves all the tasks of training, motivation, the athlete's personality and social factors 
which express and integrate the interests of the athlete, coach and team, as well as the practical experience and 
theory of training construction. In orienting the course of training in a specific direction, model characteristics are 
quantitatively assigned which relate to the training load, the athlete’s fitness state and his external interactions 
(see Fig 6.12).

The main idea of managing training consists of raising the fitness state of the body to a higher functional level. 
Control of this process is accomplished by assessing the effect at primarily two levels of management, namely at 
the level of the athlete's fitness state (control of the effect of the loading on fitness) and at the level of external 
interactions of the athlete (control of the change in their characteristics as a result of changes in fitness). Based on 
a comparison of different effects achieved at the levels indicated by the given model characteristics* suitable 
solutions are implemented in order to manage the later course of training. 
Analysis of the contents and 
organisation of training may now be summarised as follows:
1. Firstly, the interaction between the components of the managed system is determined by the training 
potential and the training effect of the loading (Fig 6.12). Here, the training potential o f the loading is 
understood to mean its potential for promoting adaptation of the body and corresponding changes in its 
fitness state and, consequently, in its external interactions. The training potential of the loading is a relative 
concept which should be examined and assessed in accordance with the athlete's current fitness state. 
Assessment o f the training effect of the loading means measuring the performance change that the loading 
produces in each case under competitive and laboratory conditions.
The training effect is achieved with relatively stable adaptation within the body, by use of any logical 
training programme. The basis for the training effect is the accumulation of adaptive traces within the body 
produced by the entire complex of training influences. The substantive meaning of training, encompassing 
the concepts of training potential and training effect of the loading has central significance for programming 
training and will be examined later in more detail.
2. The connection between the beginning and end points of training management is highly complex. The 
extent of this connection is determined primarily by the effectiveness of the operations of two 
interdependent subsystems of regulation (see Fig 6.12): {Training Load - Training Potential o f Loading - 
Athlete's Fitness State} (subsystem A) and {Training Effect o f Loading - Athlete's Fitness State • Athlete's 
External Interactions} (subsystem B). Assessment of the predictive reliability and the probability of success 
of regulation at the level of each subsystem shows one can be certain that the lower the measures for the first 
one (A), the weaker the link in the entire management system.
3. The necessity for effective management arises when there is a problem in selecting a training regime. In such 
situations success depends on the degree of accuracy in choosing the optimal from the multitude of possible 
solutions.

6.5 Prerequisites for Organising Training
A successful solution to the problem of programming and organising training cannot be obtained only by 
assembling the results of individual fragments of research. Intensive research is required to formulate usable 
concepts concerning the training process and identifying those conditions which determine its efficieni 
development. A preliminary examination of this problem already enables one to determine the goal of the task, 
the fundamental direction of research, and the specific information required (Fig 6.13).
The scheme need not be described in much detail, because its meaning and contents are sufficiently clear and 
their analysis is a matter for later discussion. Formulating a generalised theory of training requires a complcx 
approach to the organisation of research, without repeating those experimental errors which were proliferated 
during the preceding few decades.
Figure 6.13 A general theory of structuring sports training (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999).
In sport physiology especially, a divergence of the professional interests of specialists leads to the human body 
being regarded as two fairly distinct systems. Some specialists limit their study primarily to the neuromuscular 
system and its regulation by the CNS, applying their work largely to specd-strength and complex-technical types 
of sport. Others focus their interest on the cardiovascular-respiratory systems and metabolic processes which 
determine success in primarily cyclic types of sport.
Such specialisation is quite convenient for science, but is effective and applicable only on the basis of close 
integration between theory and practice. All too often, studies are based on the effect of a single factor on 
performance; very rarely does research focus on the interactive effects of concurrent or sequential complexes of 
training methods.

In particular, understanding of the scientific and practical fundamentals of the development of general 
endurance suffers. Attention is centred on the mechanism of energy production, which ignores the specialisation 
of the muscular apparatus as the direct executor of work, and general endurance is considered exclusively to be a 
(unction of respiratory potential. Therefore, physiologists were perplexed when information was revealed about 
the decrease in V02max during the competition period and the unexpectedly low V02max levels among many 
athletes in cyclic sports. However, this should not have been unexpected if they had concurrently examined the 
contractile and metabolic characteristics of the muscles of athletes who specialise in general endurance sports.
Sport training theory also abounds with misdirected efforts. Here there is a similar division in the interests of 
specialists who give preference primarily to speed-strength or cyclic sports and tend to minimise the role of 
general endurance training. This professional specialisation cannot be condemned if they limit their theoretical 
and practical generalisations to 'their' types of sport. It is when they attempt to apply the same principles and 
methods to other types of sport that this single-minded approach becomes misleading.
A definite weakness in modem sports training theory is the result of underestimating the importance of 
information obtained from physiological and biochemical research in sport, as well as from the limited amount of 
definitive scientific information which forms the basis for establishing training principles. 
Until recently, 
generalised practical experience was usually regarded as the only valid way of establishing effective training 
principles and methods, thereby neglecting the important contributions of scientific research. At the same time, 
scientists disdained this attitude and coaches regarded scientists as impractical theoreticians, with the result that 
their individual bodies of information were not shared and training methodology suffered. The advancement of 
sport now depends strongly on close cooperation between scientists, coaches and athletes.
6.6 Basic M anagem ent Theory
In most interactions in the work, social or recreational setting, leaders or managers emerge or are appointed to 
control, coordinate and guide their fellow humans to carry out certain tasks or achieve specific goals or fulfill a 
prescribed purpose.
The terms leadership and management are often used interchangeably, but there are distinct differences 
between the two, depending on the situation. Small, ephemeral groups may have leaders or elected chairpersons, 
but usually not managers. The chairman of the board of a company does not play the managerial role of the 
executive director, who in turn does not function like the sales manager, who also may act as the highly motivating 
leader of a sales team. Sports teams have captains, who are special types of leader, but they also have managers 
who have no leadership function whatsoever on the field of play. Similarly, captains usually have no prescribed 
leadership role off the field. Military officers often have to fill roles of leadership and management. What is 
common to both leadership and management is the task of marshalling together the abilities and efforts of groups of 
individuals to reach specific goals, whether social, economic, military, sporting or otherwise. What is also common 
to both is that communication is essential to the entire process.
Tellier states that management roles are determined by position in an organisation and are characterised by 
three basic elements: responsibility, authority and accountability. Leadership, on the other hand, implies power to 
influence others, which relies on factors such as expertise, personality and charisma.
Management and leadership both require an understanding of human behaviour in terms of needs, wants and 
drives, hence the next section introduces you to theories of human behaviour and motivation.
6.6.1 Human Needs and Motivation
Although many models have been formulated to explain human needs, only a few have been selected here to enable 
you to appreciate the strengths and weaknesses of each and be able to select a suitable model for a given situation 
(Siff, 1990). The motivation process involved in human drive may be summarized in the following way (Fig 6.14):
