Their rule, italicised in the original: "a diminished loading and restorative period has to be observed after a given concentrated loading phase to allow the body to supercompensate to the desired level of preparedness." The timing: "The gains elicited, for instance, by 4-8 week concentrated blocks of strength, speed-strength or speed training, may occur most commonly after a latency period of 1-3 weeks, so it is essential for the athlete not to lose patience and hasten into the next concentrated phase without adequate restoration. Not only does premature imposition of concentrated loading suppress the delayed training effect of the previous stage, but it also lowers the effectiveness of future training" (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason: "the conjugate sequence system is based on exploitation of the delayed training effect" (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294), so the next block must start once that effect has appeared, not before. No physiological mechanism is given in this section. Inference: the authors frame the restorative period as supercompensation; the two-factor (fitness-fatigue) reading in this library would describe the same pattern as fatigue clearing to reveal fitness, and the book does not choose between them here.

**When to apply** — After any 4-8 week block that concentrates on one quality, plan a lower-load period before the next concentrated block. Inference: judge the block's result after the 1-3 week latency, not on the last day of loading. Eric's baseline: "An annual plan is treated as a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 183, Inferred). Inference: the 1-3 week latency is a reason to leave slack between blocks in that roadmap, so a delayed gain is not cut short by the next block.

**When NOT to apply** — The 1-3 week figure is "most commonly," with no study named. It is a latency to the onset of gains. Chapter 6 gives a different number for a different quantity: the long-term delayed training effect "was observed to last from 4-12 weeks during the long-term stages of strength preparation," its duration "approximately equal to the duration of the strength training stage," and its appearance "individualised" (PDF p. 375 / printed p. 364, checked against the page image). **Contested across the library:** Bompa & Haff (5th ed.), not Supertraining, write that "Siff and Verkhoshansky (83) suggested that performance gains may occur 4 to 12 weeks after the cessation of the concentrated loading phase" (Bompa & Haff 5e, PDF idx 60 / printed p. 49), and the Bompa entry [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]] repeats this as a 4-12 week delay. Bompa & Haff also say that "the greater the magnitude and duration of the concentrated loading phase, the more time needed for fatigue to dissipate and performance to improve" (same page, refs 83, 91, 103, 104). Inference: read as a 4-12 week wait before gains, the Bompa & Haff sentence matches neither Supertraining statement: 5.3.3 gives a 1-3 week latency to gains (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294), and Chapter 6 gives 4-12 weeks as how long the delayed effect lasts (PDF p. 375 / printed p. 364). Read as the window in which gains show, it is close to the Chapter 6 figure. Fig 6.31 on that page (che

**Example** — The authors' own: after a 4-8 week concentrated strength block, the gains "may occur most commonly after a latency period of 1-3 weeks" (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294). Inference: an off-season strength block ending in late March would be judged in April, and the speed-emphasis block that follows would open at lower volume rather than at full load.

**Related** — [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]], [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy]] (4.1.2, the delayed training effect), [[case-study--deniskin-depth-jumps-after-resistance-and-rest-as-a-training-means]] (rest weeks between stages), [[framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]], [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]], [[claim--delayed-strength-training-effect-lag-before-gains-appear]] (4.1.1, speed-strength up 18-25% after a 10-day rest, PDF p. 213; an in-library case for a short latency), [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]]
### framework--four-level-functional-specialisation-and-special-physical-preparedness
# Functional Specialisation in Four Levels: General Abilities, Coordination, Explosive Force and Specific Endurance, Then the Structure of Special Physical Preparedness

**What it is** — Under "The Process of Functional Specialisation," the authors give "an ascending flowchart" of how the body specialises "over many years of training" (Fig 4.24, verified against the page image; PDF p. 262 / printed p. 251):
- **Level 1 (generalised abilities):** speed, strength and endurance, the "flexible mechanisms of coordination, regulation and energy production" that serve daily life and "offer extensive possibilities for adaptation."
- **Level 2:** coordination. The demands of sport "stimulate the motor function, which coordinates all muscular activity."
- **Level 3:** the ability to display explosive force, and specific endurance. "The motor function specialises chiefly by developing the ability to display explosive force and specific endurance independent of the type of sport." Specific endurance "may be predominantly cardiovascular or local muscular in nature," and explosive force relates to starting strength, acceleration-strength and absolute strength (3.2.1).
- **Level 4 (specialised abilities):** the structure of special physical preparedness, formed in "the intensive stage of functional specialisation," which "displays its own form with respect to interaction of the cardiovascular-respiratory and motor systems."

Within these structures the functional systems relate by **cooperation** ("effective interaction of all the systems") or **subordination** ("the productivity of one system is enhanced by the functional potentials of the others"). "The structure of special physical preparedness is determined by the specific training regime, and does not relate to conditions imposed by other sporting activities. This fact should be noted by anyone who may be contemplating the use of generalised cross training with various sports." (PDF pp. 262-263 / printed pp. 251-252, verified against the page images.)

**Why it works** — The authors present it as a description of the general sequence, not a tested model; the only mechanism given is that sporting demands stimulate the motor function, which then specialises. No data are attached to the flowchart.

**When to apply** — As a long-term development map: build general speed, strength and endurance and coordination first, then explosive force and specific endurance, then the sport's own structure of preparedness. Use the cross-training warning when another sport is proposed as preparation: the authors say it does not build the target sport's special preparedness. Eric's baseline: "The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill, each level a required foundation for the next)" is the department's programming "compass." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 101). Inference: both are bottom-up hierarchies that end in sport-specific ability; the Vermeil sequence orders physical qualities, while this flowchart puts coordination below explosive force and specific endurance.

**When NOT to apply** — "Independent of the type of sport" at Level 3 and "does not relate to conditions imposed by other sporting activities" at Level 4 pull in different directions: Level 3 is general across sports, Level 4 is not. The text gives no ages, durations or criteria for moving between levels. The cross-training statement is a strong claim without cited data; it addresses special preparedness, not general fitness or recovery uses of other sports.

**Example** — The book gives no worked example for the flowchart; its factor-analysis tables for high jumpers and skaters (see Related) are offered as data on the Level 4 structure.

**Related** — [[case-study--high-jumper-factor-structure-by-qualification]], [[case-study--skater-factor-structure-by-qualification]], [[principle--motor-system-leads-cardiorespiratory-adaptation-do-not-separate-them]], [[framework--key-specific-nonspecific-levelling-motor-ability-model]] (Ch2.3.4), [[claim--physical-quality-transfer-decreases-as-specific-fitness-increases]] (Ch2.3.1; agreement), [[framework--four-component-model-of-explosive-force]] (Ch3.2.1), [[framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness]] (Ch1.5); [[framework--specific-correspondence-of-the-training-effect-four-tasks]] (5.4.3, specialisation by system and by ability with four tasks; it overlaps this flowchart and adds the system-vs-ability split)
### framework--special-strength-methods-classified-by-sport-group-and-strength-type
# Classifying Special Strength Methods: Four Sport Groups, Three Effort Methods, Five Method Groups

**What it is** — The authors build the chapter's method system in three layers (PDF p. 268-269 / printed p. 257-258, verified against the page image). (1) Four categories of sport by motor regime (Diachkov 1961): sports characterised by "the production of maximal strength"; by "endurance with optimal efforts of various intensities"; by "a high level of skill"; and by "the complex display of several motor abilities at different levels of development." This grouping "identifies the primary emphasis of the strength training, which determines the choice of suitable methods," and from it come the needs for explosive strength, strength-endurance, strength-skill, relative strength and absolute strength (Diachkov 1961; Kuznetsov 1970; Chudinov 1961). It also grounds three principles: "The magnitude of the main load," "The specific need to change the training load," and "The method of incorporating into a training scheme the means for exploiting the after-effect of previous work (Verkhoshansky, 1970)." (2) Loads are split into maximal tension, speed-strength and strength-endurance loads, and maximal tension can be produced by lifting to failure or by lifting a maximal weight at maximal velocity, so "three ways of developing strength may be distinguished, i.e. repetitive, maximal and dynamic effort (Zatsiorsky, 1966)." (3) Methods are grouped by the strength they develop: "absolute strength, speed-strength, explosive strength, reactive ability and strength-endurance," and within each g

**Why it works** — The authors' rationale is that method choice should follow the motor regime of the sport, so classifying sports first makes the method choice systematic. They give no data for the scheme itself. Inference: the five method groups map onto the rest of Chapter 5 (5.2.1 maximum strength, 5.2.3 speed-strength, 5.2.4 explosive strength and reactive ability, 5.2.5 strength-endurance, per the section headings at PDF p. 269, 275, 278 and 296), which is how the book uses it.

**When to apply** — Eric's baseline (course material, Inferred): the head coach's system of play is "treated as a direct input into whether a team's programming leans toward maximal strength or toward speed/power emphasis" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 188). Inference: the four sport groups give a more formal first question for the same decision: which group does this sport, or this position, sit in? Football is the fourth group (several abilities at different levels), and positions differ inside it, so a lineman and a receiver may draw from different method groups.

**When NOT to apply** — The four-group classification is a 1961 scheme that the authors adopt without data. Inference: many team sports fall into group 4 by default, so the grouping says little there; the position-level demand matters more. The three effort methods are cited to Zatsiorsky 1966 only by name on this page; the book does not define "dynamic effort" here, so (Inference) do not read a later, narrower meaning of "dynamic effort" into it from this passage.

**Example** — The authors' own example list of strength types derived from the grouping: explosive strength, strength-endurance and strength-skill (Diachkov 1961; Kuznetsov 1970), and relative strength, absolute strength and strength-endurance (Chudinov 1961) (PDF p. 269 / printed p. 258).

**Related** — [[framework--three-methods-for-maximum-strength-repetitive-brief-maximal-isometric]] (5.2.1); [[framework--two-groups-of-speed-strength-movements-and-their-tension-types]] (5.2.3); [[framework--eight-types-of-muscular-tension]] (3.1, the contraction types used inside each group); [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]; [[framework--post-activation-potentiation-load-timing-sequencing]] (the after-effect principle)
### claim--vo2max-alone-does-not-determine-endurance-performance
# VO2 Max on Its Own Does Not Decide Endurance Results: Equal VO2 Max, Different Results; Stable VO2 Max, Rising Results; Falling VO2 Max in the Competition Period

**What it is** — The authors argue that analysing endurance "solely at the level of the cardiovascular-respiratory and motor systems is inadequate," especially when endurance is reduced to respiratory function and VO2 max, and that endurance methods "are still based on such ideas" (PDF p. 259 / printed p. 248). Three groups of evidence:
1. Athletes with equal VO2 max show different results, and the reverse. "Top middle-distance runners of the 1940s had the same VO2 max as today's athletes, yet there are major differences in performance (Faulkner, 1968)." There are "no statistically reliable differences between athletes of different qualification" in aerobic potential, but "significant differences with respect to anaerobic efficiency" (Nabotnikova 1972; Serafimova 1974; Rusko 1976).
2. VO2 max stabilises in highly qualified athletes while results improve: the best Soviet and Swedish skaters over 4-5 years (Orlov & Sharova 1977); qualified road cyclists over many years (Melenberg et al 1972).
3. VO2 max falls significantly in the competition period in cyclists, swimmers, skiers, skaters, middle-distance runners and hockey players (citations for each, PDF p. 259 / printed p. 248), and its correlation with results falls from "R = 0.7 during the preparation period" to "0.4 during the competitive period" (Vasiliev & Trunin 1974; Melenberg 1981; PDF p. 260 / printed p. 249, verified against the page image).

They conclude "VO2 max on its own is no guarantee of outstanding performance," and that other factors count, "such as the ability to perform work for a prolonged period at a level of oxygen consumption close to the VO2 max, and the ability to effectively utilise available energy under competitive conditions" (PDF p. 260 / printed p. 249).

**Why it works** — For the competition-period fall in VO2 max the authors offer two possible explanations, "the decreasing trainability of aerobic processes or ... an inherent antagonism between aerobic and anaerobic processes (Zatsiorsky et al, 1974; Volkov, 1975)" (PDF p. 260 / printed p. 249). One page later they say the antagonism assumption "must be questioned" (Mellenberg & Khvan 1982; PDF pp. 260-261 / printed pp. 249-250) and explain the fall through blood-flow changes instead (see [[claim--local-blood-flow-not-vo2max-tracks-competition-period-endurance-gains]]). Both are kept here because the text gives both.

**When to apply** — When a coach or test battery treats VO2 max as the main endurance marker: also measure sustained work near VO2 max, anaerobic capacity, and sport-specific work capacity, and do not read a stable or falling VO2 max in season as lost fitness by itself. Eric's baseline: conditioning is defined as meeting the sport's energy requirements and sustaining "strength, speed, and power output across a full competition." **Explicit** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 113). Inference: that definition already points away from a single aerobic marker, in line with this section.

**When NOT to apply** — The evidence is a list of mostly Soviet citations from 1968-1981 summarised in a sentence each, with no sample sizes or methods given, and the correlation drop (0.7 to 0.4) is reported without the sport or sample. The 1940s comparison mixes eras with different training, tracks and competition depth. This does not show VO2 max is unimportant: the authors themselves recommend raising it (see the contested entry in Related).

**Example** — The book's own: qualified road cyclists whose VO2 max stayed "practically unchanged ... over many years of training, yet their performances improved" (Melenberg et al 1972; PDF p. 259 / printed p. 248).

**Related** — [[claim--endurance-rests-on-muscle-oxidative-and-strength-qualities-not-vo2max]], [[claim--local-blood-flow-not-vo2max-tracks-competition-period-endurance-gains]], [[case-study--skater-factor-structure-by-qualification]] (Table 4.2, aerobic factors' share falls at Master of Sport level), [[claim--energy-system-contribution-by-sport-table]].

# A General-Preparation Stage Only "Counts" If It Lasts as Long as the Athlete's Own Sports-Form Cycle

**What it is** — Bondarchuk states that most athletes, after a rest/transition period,
take 2-3 months to enter a state of "sports form" in whatever exercises they are doing,
though some individuals take "4-7 and even 8 months" (PDF p. 39, printed p. 22). A
general-preparation stage/block can only function as a real "base" or "foundation" for the
following specialized stage if it lasts at least as long as that individual's own
sports-form development timeline. He gives his own worked numbers for how this plays out:
in a single-cycle training year, the general-preparation stage runs "on the average, three
months," long enough to let most athletes actually enter sports form in it; in a two-cycle
year, the second general-preparation stage shrinks to "4-6 weeks," and in a three-cycle
year to "2-3 weeks", both too short for athletes to "have time to enter into full sports
form in the exercises used." (PDF pp. 39-40, printed pp. 22-23.) He gives a
worked counter-example: a sprint/hurdle program with a 10-day general-endurance stage, a
15-day general-strength stage, a 6-8 week speed/speed-endurance stage, and a 2-3 week
entry-into-form stage. Because the first two stages are far shorter than the 2-3+ months
needed to reach sports form, he argues it is "impossible to resolve" real development of

### block-periodization--issurin/case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles
# Case Study: Bondarchuk's Developmental/Competitive/Restorative Blocks and the 1988 Hammer Throw Podium

**What it is** — Issurin credits Anatoly Bondarchuk, hammer-throw coach, with one of the
precursor systems to Block Periodization (PDF p. 32, printed p. 21). Based on his own
athletic career (1972 Olympic hammer-throw champion) and doctoral research on throwers'
training programs (1988), Bondarchuk built a periodization chart using three types of
specialized mesocycle-blocks: **developmental** (workload gradually increases to maximum),
**competitive** (load stabilizes, athletes focus on competitive performance), and
**restorative** (active recovery, preparing for the next developmental block). Stated
durations: developmental and competitive blocks are "usually four weeks," restorative "can
be shortened to two weeks." Sequencing depends on the competition schedule and individual
athlete response. The book also gives what it calls Bondarchuk's design's outstanding
characteristic: alternation and repetition of the exercise repertory in each mesocycle-block
(every four weeks); the traditional period names, preparatory, competitive, and transitory,
were kept, but Bondarchuk noted that in his concept "their essence is very different" (as
reported by Issurin, PDF p. 32, printed p. 21). The claimed outcome: Bondarchuk coached the gold, silver, and bronze
medalists in hammer throw at the 1988 and other Olympic Games, "the entire Olympic podium
occupied by athletes of the same coach" (Bondarchuk, 1986 and 1988, as cited by Issurin).

does not describe Bondarchuk's own stated reasoning for why these particular block lengths

introduced conceptually in [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]
(Ch. 1). Issurin gives duration as a function of two competing factors (PDF pp. 113-115,
printed pp. 102-104): the time needed for a real cumulative training effect in the targeted

weeks added only 0.25% and then 0.13% per week. Issurin's stated conclusion: the fitness
program was "very effective at the beginning, reasonably effective through the first six

### periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching
# Concentrated Loading and Planned Overreaching

**What it is** — A short period of deliberately high, "saturated" training load on one quality (planned overreaching), followed by restitution. Performance is *suppressed* during the loading block and rebounds — supercompensates — afterward. Bompa & Haff cite Siff and Verkhoshansky for gains **4 to 12 weeks** after the concentrated block ends (Bompa & Haff 5e, printed p. 49); *Supertraining* itself gives a 1-3 week latency before gains appear and 4-12 weeks as how long the delayed effect lasts (see [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]]). Bompa & Haff's own rule (same page): the longer/larger the loading, the longer the delay before performance lifts. The **conjugated sequence** extends this: concentrate on one emphasis (e.g. strength) while holding maintenance loads elsewhere, then shift emphasis in the unloading block so a different quality rises.

**Why it works** — Saturating a stimulus drives a deeper adaptive signal than steady loading. Monitoring via the **testosterone:cortisol (T:C) ratio** tracks the anabolic–catabolic balance: ≥3 weeks of concentrated load lowers the basal T:C ratio (a catabolic shift, reduced preparedness); returning load to normal lets the T:C ratio and performance supercompensate. T:C indexes *preparedness*, not overtraining per se.

**When to apply** — Advanced athletes who can tolerate high loads; building a potent stimulus before a taper/peak; reducing long-term work volume versus concurrent training; timing a delayed performance rebound to a competition window.

**When NOT to apply** — Not for novices or athletes without the training capacity to absorb saturating loads — fatigue is substantial during accum
### periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle
# The Supercompensation Cycle

**What it is** — After a training stimulus the body passes through four phases: (I) fatigue/homeostasis drop, 1–2 hr; (II) compensation/recovery, 24–48 hr; (III) supercompensation — a rebound *above* baseline, ~36–72 hr; (IV) involution — the gain fades if no new stimulus arrives, 3–7 days. Training the next stimulus into the supercompensation window raises the homeostatic set-point over time. Also called Weigert's law; Bompa links it to Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (alarm → resistance → exhaustion).

**Why it works** — A bout depletes substrates (glycogen, PCr), accumulates fatigue and cortisol, and transiently lowers force output. Given adequate recovery the body overshoots when restoring those reserves, establishing a new, higher baseline. Protein synthesis is elevated +50% by 4 hr and +109% by 24 hr post-resistance-bout.

**When to apply** — Sequencing hard sessions and recovery; justifying why intensities must alternate (high/moderate/low); timing the next stressor to land on the rebound, not the trough.

**When NOT to apply** — Don't treat it as a precise single-factor clock. Recovery windows vary enormously by session type (6–8 hr for medium aerobic work; >48 hr for high-CNS work) and by athlete training status, nutrition, and contraction type (eccentric/SSC fatigue recovers bimodally, full recovery 6–8 days). Contemporary sport science largely prefers the **fitness–fatigue (two-factor) model** over literal supercompensation; treat this as a useful mental model, not a measured prescription. See [[principle--progressive-overload-threshold]] and [[heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]].

### ../../../../DEV/Flint/staging/library/strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing
# The Two-Factor Model Can Be Formalized Mathematically, and Its Research Base Argues Against Heavy Training Right Before Competition

**What it is** — The Two-Factor (Fitness-Fatigue) Model treats preparedness at time t as
initial preparedness plus the summed effect of a slow-decaying fitness after-effect and a
faster-decaying fatigue after-effect, each with its own magnitude and decay-time constant
(Banister et al., 1992). Banister and Calvert (1980) originated this with the Training
Impulse (TRIMP), a quantified unit of training load used to model and predict elite
swimming performance from the fitness/fatigue balance. Zatsiorsky (1995) is cited for the
same 3:1 fitness-to-fatigue decay ratio already in this library's Bompa material. Later
research building on this model examined tapering specifically: Fitz-Clarke et al. (1991)
found presently accepted taper protocols may be too rigorous and short for best results,
and several studies (Zarkadas et al. 1995; Mujika et al. 1996; Shepley et al. 1992) found
that proper placement of training volume during a taper is a key optimization factor, with
high training volume in the days immediately preceding competition possibly detrimental to
performance. Different muscle groups recover heterochronically, which is why some Russian
restoration specialists deliberately avoid applying restorative methods (e.g. massage) to
every muscle group after every session, since supercompensation is reportedly more
pronounced with partial rather than total restoration. (PDF pp. 99-100, printed pp. 88-89.)

**Why it works** — Modeling preparedness as the sum of two exponentially-decaying
after-effects with different time constants gives periodization a quantitative structure

# Concentrated Loading and Planned Overreaching

**What it is** — A short period of deliberately high, "saturated" training load on one quality (planned overreaching), followed by restitution. Performance is *suppressed* during the loading block and rebounds — supercompensates — afterward. Bompa & Haff cite Siff and Verkhoshansky for gains **4 to 12 weeks** after the concentrated block ends (Bompa & Haff 5e, printed p. 49); *Supertraining* itself gives a 1-3 week latency before gains appear and 4-12 weeks as how long the delayed effect lasts (see [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]]). Bompa & Haff's own rule (same page): the longer/larger the loading, the longer the delay before performance lifts. The **conjugated sequence** extends this: concentrate on one emphasis (e.g. strength) while holding maintenance loads elsewhere, then shift emphasis in the unloading block so a different quality rises.

**Why it works** — Saturating a stimulus drives a deeper adaptive signal than steady loading. Monitoring via the **testosterone:cortisol (T:C) ratio** tracks the anabolic–catabolic balance: ≥3 weeks of concentrated load lowers the basal T:C ratio (a catabolic shift, reduced preparedness); returning load to normal lets the T:C ratio and performance supercompensate. T:C indexes *preparedness*, not overtraining per se.

**When to apply** — Advanced athletes who can tolerate high loads; building a potent stimulus before a taper/peak; reducing long-term work volume versus concurrent training; timing a delayed performance rebound to a competition window.

### periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle
# The Supercompensation Cycle

**What it is** — After a training stimulus the body passes through four phases: (I) fatigue/homeostasis drop, 1–2 hr; (II) compensation/recovery, 24–48 hr; (III) supercompensation — a rebound *above* baseline, ~36–72 hr; (IV) involution — the gain fades if no new stimulus arrives, 3–7 days. Training the next stimulus into the supercompensation window raises the homeostatic set-point over time. Also called Weigert's law; Bompa links it to Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (alarm → resistance → exhaustion).

**Why it works** — A bout depletes substrates (glycogen, PCr), accumulates fatigue and cortisol, and transiently lowers force output. Given adequate recovery the body overshoots when restoring those reserves, establishing a new, higher baseline. Protein synthesis is elevated +50% by 4 hr and +109% by 24 hr post-resistance-bout.

**When to apply** — Sequencing hard sessions and recovery; justifying why intensities must alternate (high/moderate/low); timing the next stressor to land on the rebound, not the trough.

**When NOT to apply** — Don't treat it as a precise single-factor clock. Recovery windows vary enormously by session type (6–8 hr for medium aerobic work; >48 hr for high-CNS work) and by athlete training status, nutrition, and contraction type (eccentric/SSC fatigue recovers bimodally, full recovery 6–8 days). Contemporary sport science largely prefers the **fitness–fatigue (two-factor) model** over literal supercompensation; treat this as a useful mental model, not a measured prescription. See [[principle--progressive-overload-threshold]] and [[heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]].

**What it is** — The Two-Factor (Fitness-Fatigue) Model treats preparedness at time t as
initial preparedness plus the summed effect of a slow-decaying fitness after-effect and a
faster-decaying fatigue after-effect, each with its own magnitude and decay-time constant
(Banister et al., 1992). Banister and Calvert (1980) originated this with the Training

# Biochemical Adaptations Occur in a Fixed Order, and Reverse in the Opposite Order When Training Stops

**What it is** — Citing Platonov (1988), the authors state biochemical adaptation to
training follows a definite three-stage sequence, not a simultaneous shift: first,
oxidative ATP resynthesis potential and glycogen level increase; next, structural muscle
protein (myosin) and the intensity of non-oxidative ATP resynthesis (glycolysis) increase;

disrupted acid-base balance. (PD

6.2.3 The Relationship between Intensity and Volume
Studies have shown that, in the annual macrocycle, the weekly levels of volume and intensity coincide fairly 
closely in sports requiring strength (Chernyak et al, 1979). Generally, the largest number of weeks involve 
medium volume and medium intensity, as well as weeks with high volume and high intensity. Chernyak's 
research produced the following recommendations for strength-speed sports:
1. It is inadvisable always to combine low volume with low intensity, medium volume with medium intensity 
and large volume with high intensity.
2. Training is most effective and least injurious if:
• medium volume, medium intensity loading is used most frequently (about 12-15 weeks per year)
• medium or high volume, low intensity loading is used next most frequently (9-10 weeks per year)
• low volume, medium intensity loading is then most commonly applied (6-7 weeks per year).
3. Other combinations should be applied even less frequently, such as:
• large volume, medium intensity (3-4 weeks)
• large volume, high intensity (2-3 weeks)
• low volume, high intensity (3-4 weeks)
• low volume, low intensity (1-2 weeks).
However, it should be remembered that the overall volume and intensity of any load tell us little about the loading 
imposed in different intensity zones or at the level of individual muscle groups. Nor does it say anything about
SUPERTRAINING
the individual’s perceived response to loading, as discussed earlier. Therefore, it is always to pay attention to 
these details, as well as the level of mastery of the athlete, in devising an effective training programme.
6.3 The Periodisation Controversy
The widespread Western use of classical periodisation along the lines originally pioneered by Matveyev may 
create the impression that it should be regarded as the pre-eminent and most appropriate method of organising 
long term training. 
However, even among Russian researchers and scientists, this approach to training has 
attracted some fierce criticism.
Some of this criticism is warranted, such as the belief that periodisation is an exact science in which all 
training may be prescribed via the use of computerised programmes based upon exact calculations of intensity 
and volume of every training session, microcycle and longer term cycle. The body is not an exactly controlled, 
deterministic system, but its subsystems are attracted to and deviate from approximate states of balance which 
show continual variation

imposed in different intensity zones or at the level of individual muscle groups. Nor does it say anything about

the individual’s perceived response to loading, as discussed earlier. Therefore, it is always to pay attention to 
these details, as well as the level of mastery of the athlete, in devising an effective training programme.
6.3 The Periodisation Controversy
The widespread Western use of classical periodisation along the lines originally pioneered by Matveyev may 
create the impression that it should be regarded as the pre-eminent and most appropriate method of organising 
long term training. 
However, even among Russian researchers and scientists, this approach to training has 
attracted some fierce criticism.
Some of this criticism is warranted, such as the belief that periodisation is an exact science in which all 
training may be prescribed via the use of computerised programmes based upon exact calculations of intensity 
and volume of every training session, microcycle and longer term cycle. The body is not an exactly controlled, 
deterministic system, but its subsystems are attracted to and deviate from approximate states of balance which

26:This review distinguishes concentrated-unidirectional and multi-targeted block models and provides a useful conceptual vocabulary for discussing concentrated workloads and sequencing.
34:- The review emphasizes elite, subelite, and well-trained athletes across endurance, team, combat, dual, jumping, and strength/power settings. [p. 11]
40:- Narrative review contrasting concentrated-unidirectional and multi-targeted block-periodization models.
46:- Concentrated-unidirectional programs in combat and team sports improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team practice or competitive performance. [p. 6]
47:- In an elite-swimmer example, specific strength and anaerobic capacity improved but swimming performance improved in only two of three athletes. [p. 6]
48:- The author judged the concentrated-unidirectional evidence insufficient for broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation. [p. 6]
49:- The review reports support from 28 studies for multi-targeted block programs, but the designs, populations, outcomes, and comparator quality varied. [p. 11]
50:- The concentrated-unidirectional model was presented as better suited to sports dominated by a narrow target quality and as restricted when peak performance requires many interacting abilities. [p. 11]
51:- Whose model is whose: the concentrated-unidirectional (CU) model is Verkhoshansky's; the multi-targeted model with 28-study support is Issurin's own A-T-R block model. [pp. 6-7, 11] So this review does not dispute Issurin's 2008 book; it repeats the book's critique of traditional planning. The real 2008-2016 difference is on lower-level athletes: the book (p. 33) says they do fine with medium concentration, while this review says "no evidence that amateur athletes have any serious restrictions" with highly concentrated block workloads. [p. 11] (Clarified 2026-09-27 during the Flint review of Issurin's book, checked against the paper pages.)
56:- Fitness improvements are not interchangeable with sport-specific performance, availability, or competitive outcomes. [p. 6]
59:- The strong conclusion favoring multi-targeted block periodization is the author's synthesis and should not be treated as settled comparative evidence. [p. 11]
63:Use block periodization as a planning hypothesis: concentrate compatible emphases when competition structure and athlete needs justify it, while maintaining the qualities and technical exposure that cannot safely decay. Judge the plan by sport-specific performance, availability, and individual response—not by the periodization label. Compare it prospectively with the program's own prior practice where feasible.
69:| Review scope and distinction between two models | p. 4 | narrative framing |
70:| Concentrated-unidirectional evidence and performance gaps | p. 6 | narrative synthesis |
71:| Multi-targeted evidence claim and applicability boundaries | p. 11 | narrative synthesis/limitation |
76:- [[training-load-concentration]] — sequencing compatible emphases
77:- [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]]: Supertraining 5.3.3's system of successive concentrated blocks; it cites this review's limits for team, combat and swimming preparation as the case against using that system there

---
type: library-entry
kind: framework
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "6.4"
topic: training as a management system
category: [programming, monitoring, training-load, theory]
confidence: untested
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-10-03
---

# Training as a Managed System: Training Load, Fitness State and External Interactions, Controlled at Two Levels

**What it is** — The authors treat programming "as a problem in management" and name three components of the managed system (PDF p. 347 / printed p. 336, checked against the page image):
1. "The complex of the athlete's external influences encountered in competition." "The greater the athlete's motor potential, the more effectively the complex of external interactions can be organised." Sports results "are the observable product of the organisation of the athlete's external interactions."
2. "the athlete's fitness state," defined as "the athlete's structural-functional qualities which determine the athlete's potential to produce sporting prowess (Zatsiorsky, 1979)."
3. "specialised motor activities, i.e. the training load."

The causal chain runs one way: "The dosage of the training load is prescribed to promote changes in the athlete's fitness state which, in turn, entails changes in the complex of external interactions of the athlete and a corresponding improvement in sporting results." When planned results are reached, "the sequence of the preceding conditions is repeated at higher levels" (PDF p. 347 / printed p. 336).

Fig 6.12, "A logical scheme for organising sports training (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999)" (PDF p. 348 / printed p. 337, checked against the page image), draws the loop: Fitness needs for given sport, Training objectives, Programming of training, Characteristics of training model, then Training load, Training potential of loading, Athlete's fitness state (shaded box A), Training effect of loading, Athlete's external interactions (shaded box B), Change in performance, and Assessment of effect (fed by "Sports Competition" and "Laboratory Tests"), which returns to Fitness needs.

Key terms (PDF p. 348 / printed p. 337):
- **Training potential of the loading:** "its potential for promoting adaptation of the body and corresponding changes in its fitness state," and "a relative concept which should be examined and assessed in accordance with the athlete's current fitness state."
- **Assessment of the training effect:** "measuring the performance change that the loading produces in each case under competitive and laboratory conditions."
- **Two levels of control:** the fitness state ("control of the effect of the loading on fitness") and external interactions ("control of the change in their characteristics as a result of changes in fitness").
- **Two subsystems:** A = {Training Load, Training Potential of Loading, Athlete's Fitness State}; B = {Training Effect of Loading, Athlete's Fitness State, Athlete's External Interactions}. "the lower the measures for the first one (A), the weaker the link in the entire management system."

**Why it works** — The authors' reason is structural: fitness state is the only route from load to result, so both the load-to-fitness link and the fitness-to-performance link must be measured. The basis for the training effect is "the accumulation of adaptive traces within the body produced by the entire complex of training influences" (PDF p. 348 / printed p. 337). They give no data for the scheme; it is a conceptual model, hence `untested`.

**When to apply** — Auditing a monitoring set-up: for each test, ask which box of Fig 6.12 it measures. A jump test reads the fitness state; game or practice output reads external interactions; neither alone closes the loop. Eric's baseline: "Preparedness (the athlete's underlying physical capability, built over a long period) is explicitly distinguished from readiness (day-to-day fluctuation)" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 64, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the authors' "fitness state" corresponds to that preparedness, and the two-level control is the same split between what the body can do and what it shows in competition. Eric's baseline: "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place" (line 32, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q3)). Inference: Fig 6.12 gives each test a place to answer to: a test that sits in no box of the loop is the kind the rule removes.

**When NOT to apply** — The scheme names what to measure but gives no measures, thresholds or numbers. "One can be certain that the lower the measures for the first one (A), the weaker the link" is stated without a study. The authors also widen "management" in the same passage to "motivation, the athlete's personality and social factors" (PDF p. 347 / printed p. 336), which the figure does not show. Inference: the model is linear and single-athlete; it does not cover fatigue, injury or sport-skill learning as separate inputs.

**Example** — The authors give no worked case. Inference: a sprinter's training load (sprints, jumps, lifts) is assessed at level A by laboratory tests (jump height, isometric force) and at level B by race times; if the tests rise but race times do not, the weak link is between fitness state and external interactions, not the load.

**Related** — [[framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy]], [[framework--four-level-functional-specialisation-and-special-physical-preparedness]], [[framework--specific-correspondence-of-the-training-effect-four-tasks]], [[heuristic--build-training-theory-from-interacting-complexes-and-coach-scientist-cooperation]] (6.5, the research programme behind Fig 6.13), [[old-bull-performance-course--old-bull/framework--monitoring-versus-testing]]

# Training Theory Needs Research on Interacting Complexes of Means and Close Coach-Scientist Cooperation, Not Single-Factor Fragments

**What it is** — The authors open 6.5: "A successful solution to the problem of programming and organising training cannot be obtained only by assembling the results of individual fragments of research" (PDF p. 349 / printed p. 338, checked against the page image). Their diagnosis has three parts:
1. **Split specialists.** Some study "primarily ... the neuromuscular system," applying it "largely to speed-strength and complex-technical types of sport"; others the "cardiovascular-respiratory systems and metabolic processes" of cyclic sports. Such specialisation "is effective and applicable only on the basis of close integration between theory and practice."
2. **Single-factor designs.** "All too often, studies are based on the effect of a single factor on performance; very rarely does research focus on the interactive effects of concurrent or sequential complexes of training methods" (PDF p. 349 / printed p. 338).
3. **Over-generalising across sport types.** Specialists who favour speed-strength or cyclic sports cannot be condemned "if they limit their theoretical and practical generalisations to 'their' types of sport. It is when they attempt to apply the same principles and methods to other types of sport that this single-minded approach becomes misleading" (PDF p. 350 / printed p. 339, checked against the page image).

On the coach-scientist divide: "Until recently, generalised practical experience was usually regarded as the only valid way of establishing effective training principles," while "scientists disdained this attitude and coaches regarded scientists as impractical theoreticians, with the result that their individual bodies of information were not shared and training methodology suffered. The advancement of sport now depends strongly on close cooperation between scientists, coaches and athletes" (PDF p. 350 / printed p. 339).

Fig 6.13, "A general theory of structuring sports training (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999)" (PDF p. 349 / printed p. 338, checked against the page image), lays out the research agenda: The Training Process splits into Programming (characteristics of adaptation; of structural-functional specialisation; of the athlete's state and training load; of attaining sports mastery), Organisation (interdependence of training and competitive activities; classification of loads by emphasis and training potential; optimal duration and interdependence of loads of different emphasis) and Management (methods of assessing the athlete's state; of calculating and analysing loads; models of the dynamics of the athlete's state). These lead to principles of structuring, ways of structuring, and ways of controlling and correcting training, which feed a "General theory of training construction," together with "Concepts of training in given sports" and "Principles of individualising training."

**Why it works** — The authors' example of the cost of the divide: because general endurance was treated "exclusively to be a function of respiratory potential," physiologists "were perplexed" by the fall in VO2 max in the competition period, which "should not have been unexpected if they had concurrently examined the contractile and metabolic characteristics of the muscles" (PDF p. 350 / printed p. 339). That argument is atomized from Chapter 4 in [[claim--vo2max-alone-does-not-determine-endurance-performance]]. No further mechanism is given; this is the authors' methodological position.

**When to apply** — Reading or commissioning research: prefer studies of combined and sequenced programmes over one-variable studies, and check that a finding comes from the same sport group before transferring it. Eric's baseline: Applied Performance's mission is to "drive elite performance ... by leveraging science and technology through education and relationships" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 27, Explicit). Inference: the authors' call for "close cooperation between scientists, coaches and athletes" is the same stance, stated from the research side. Eric's baseline: "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention" (line 30, Explicit). Inference: the authors' Fig 6.13 is a research wish-list; the baseline's cost rule decides which parts of it a department can afford to measure.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors give no survey or count behind "All too often" or "very rarely"; these are judgments. Single-factor studies are still the way to establish a mechanism, and the authors do not say they are useless, only insufficient on their own. Fig 6.13 is a scheme the authors say "need not be described in much detail," with no data (PDF p. 349 / printed p. 338).

**Example** — The authors' own: the VO2 max fall in the competition period, which puzzled specialists who studied only respiration but would have been expected by anyone also studying the working muscles (PDF p. 350 / printed p. 339).

# The Arousal Optimum Is Individual: Fit Restoration to Personality and Task Complexity, and Do Not Read the Yerkes-Dodson Curve Literally

**What it is** — The model is Yerkes and Dodson's inverted-U of performance against arousal; the authors borrow it and apply it to training stress and restoration. The 6.6.1 section cites "(Siff, 1990)" as the source of its selection of models; this entry still writes "the authors" because no passage names Verkhoshansky in the third person. The authors' points (PDF p. 351 / printed p. 340, checked against the page image, unless noted):
1. **The optimum is individual.** "There appears to be an optimum level of arousal for any person performing a specific task at a specific time." The curve's shape "depends on individual characteristics such as level of introversion/extroversion, level of exhaustion, standard of health, and task complexity," and "all motivational techniques are not universally applicable to everyone."
2. **Personality and restoration.** "the introvert appears to have a lower optimal arousal zone, unlike the extrovert who requires greater stimulation and can cope better with high levels of stress." This "has important implications for the prescription of restorative procedures, with the introvert probably requiring early restoration and the extrovert requiring careful monitoring to prevent overtraining caused by a desire for greater stimulation."
3. **Task complexity.** "Complex tasks require low levels of arousal to reach optimal performance over very limited periods (e.g. in golf, gymnastics and pole vaulting), whereas simple sports tasks may be executed over a longer period at higher levels of arousal." Applied to training: "Excessive exposure of an athlete to complex training tasks can lead rapidly to 'overstress', while simple tasks may be insufficiently challenging to produce continued supercompensation. A balance between complexity, simplicity, intensity and volume of load is necessary to ensure growth and to minimise overtraining" (PDF pp. 351-352 / printed pp. 340-341).
4. **Repeated stress changes the response.** "regular exposure to a stressor may produce either habituation or oversensitisation, so that the same level of stress may not produce the same response at a later stage. In either event, timely use of restoration measures is of central importance."
5. **Limits of the curve.** It "implies that there is just one discrete peak"; the "'second wind' phenomenon (curve B) and the effect of task complexity on curve shape are two of several reasons why the original curve must be applied to restoration and stress management with circumspection." Also, "it is well known that both sensory underload and overload may lead to phases of enhanced performance (curves A, C)," and meditation and similar states "may enhance performance in certain situations (curve A)." Hence "both optimisation and transcendental stress management strategies are necessary."

Fig 6.15 (checked against the page image) is a schematic with no units: one broad inverted-U over "low / optimal / high" arousal, a narrow spike A at low arousal, and spikes B and C near high arousal.

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism and no data for the introvert/extrovert or task-complexity claims; point 2 is hedged ("appears", "probably"), and the "it is well known" sentence in point 5 carries no citation.

**When to apply** — When an athlete's response to the same load differs from a teammate's: consider temperament and task complexity before changing the load. Technical sessions (high complexity) may need calm conditions and short exposures; simple conditioning can tolerate higher arousal for longer. Eric's baseline: "Recovery is managed through training-load design alone; nothing objective is tracked, sleep included" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 153, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)). Inference: the authors' point 2 suggests that load design alone may under-serve the athletes who need restoration early, and point 4 says the same load can stop meaning the same thing over a season.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not sort athletes into introvert and extrovert recovery plans on this basis: the authors give no study, and their own wording is tentative. Inference: personality typing is a weak predictor next to measured response; a measured fatigue marker is the better trigger for restoration. The figure's curves A, B and C are illustrations, not data. The task-complexity claim is about arousal during performance; the jump to "complex training tasks ... 'overstress'" is the authors' extension, also without data.

**Example** — The authors' own: golf, gymnastics and pole vaulting as complex tasks needing low arousal over very limited periods (PDF p. 351 / printed p. 340). Inference: a pole vaulter's technical session is kept short and calm, while the same athlete's sprint conditioning tolerates a louder, longer session.

type: library-entry
kind: heuristic
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "6.6.1"
topic: expectancy theory of motivation
category: [psychology, motivation, coaching, goal-setting]
confidence: untested
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-10-03
---

# Expectancy Motivation: Effort Follows Attractiveness Times Believed Attainability, So Break Distant Goals Into Reachable Steps

**What it is** — The model is Vroom's Expectancy Theory of Motivation, which the authors take from Tellier (1978) and apply to coaching athletes (PDF p. 353 / printed p. 342, checked against the page image). "it is not merely a specific goal, but the individual perception of that goal which motivates people." Motivational Force depends on:
- "the perceived attractiveness (valence V) of the goal or outcome"
- "the perceived probability of achieving that goal or outcome (one's personal belief, B, that success is likely)"

combined as "their arithmetic product F = V X B." Scales: attractiveness "from -5 (extremely undesirable) to +5 (extremely desirable)," belief "from 0 (total disbelief) to 1 (total belief)"; the overall force "is the sum of the motivational forces calculated from the products ... for all the important goals or outcomes associated with carrying out the task."

The authors' applications: if a goal is "extremely attractive, but you believe it to be far outside your reach, you will experience a small Motivational Force," so "it is desirable to break down a large or distant goal into smaller goals to be achieved over a period or at a rate which you perceive to be more matched to your capabilities or experience." And: "a manager or leader can motivate athletes strongly if he appreciates that motivation depends on perceptions of goal attractiveness and attainability. He can improve performance either by modifying the task accordingly or by altering the athlete's perceptions of the task and its outcomes" (PDF p. 353 / printed p. 342).

**Why it works** — The mechanism is the multiplication itself: if belief is near zero, attractiveness cannot compensate. The authors give no study and say "Detailed examples of this theory are outside the scope of this book" (PDF p. 353 / printed p. 342).

**When to apply** — Setting targets with an athlete: check both terms. A target the athlete values but does not believe in (a large testing jump, a return-to-play date) gets split into stages the athlete can see as reachable. A target the athlete can reach but does not value needs its outcome made worth something to that athlete. Eric's baseline: "New movement patterns are expected to take roughly 3-4 weeks of practice to become efficient" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 171, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: that expected timeline is one way to keep belief realistic when a new exercise is introduced, so early clumsiness is not read as failure.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors present the model without data, and the scales (-5 to +5, 0 to 1) are Vroom's as reported, not measured here. The page gives F as a single product and then as a sum over outcomes; both appear, for one goal and for a task with several outcomes. "Altering the athlete's perceptions" is not licence to inflate belief beyond the athlete's real capability; Inference: a target that is then missed lowers belief for the next one.

**Example** — The authors' own, in general form: a goal that is highly attractive but believed far out of reach yields little effort until it is broken into smaller goals matched to capability (PDF p. 353 / printed p. 342). Inference: an athlete told to add 100 kg to a squat over a year is given four quarterly targets instead.

**Related** — [[heuristic--arousal-optimum-is-individual-so-fit-restoration-to-personality-and-task-complexity]], [[framework--situational-leadership-coach-matches-style-to-athlete-maturity]], [[claim--plyometric-skill-is-cognitive-and-state-dependent]], [[research-papers/halson-2017-amazing-athletes-with-ordinary-habits-why-is-changing-behavior-so-difficult]]

# Expectancy Motivation: Effort Follows Attractiveness Times Believed Attainability, So Break Distant Goals Into Reachable Steps

**What it is** — The model is Vroom's Expectancy Theory of Motivation, which the authors take from Tellier (1978) and apply to coaching athletes (PDF p. 353 / printed p. 342, checked against the page image). "it is not merely a specific goal, but the individual perception of that goal which motivates people." Motivational Force depends on:
- "the perceived attractiveness (valence V) of the goal or outcome"
- "the perceived probability of achieving that goal or outcome (one's personal belief, B, that success is likely)"

combined as "their arithmetic product F = V X B." Scales: attractiveness "from -5 (extremely undesirable) to +5 (extremely desirable)," belief "from 0 (total disbelief) to 1 (total belief)"; the overall force "is the sum of the motivational forces calculated from the products ... for all the important goals or outcomes associated with carrying out the task."

The authors' applications: if a goal is "extremely attractive, but you believe it to be far outside your reach, you will experience a small Motivational Force," so "it is desirable to break down a large or distant goal into smaller goals to be achieved over a period or at a rate which you perceive to be more matched to your capabilities or experience." And: "a manager or leader can motivate athletes strongly if he appreciates that motivation depends on perceptions of goal attractiveness and attainability. He can improve performance either by modifying the task accordingly or by altering the athlete's perceptions of the task and its outcomes" (PDF p. 353 / printed p. 342).

**Why it works** — The mechanism is the multiplication itself: if belief is near zero, attractiveness cannot compensate. The authors give no study and say "Detailed examples of this theory are outside the scope of this book" (PDF p. 353 / printed p. 342).

**When to apply** — Setting targets with an athlete: check both terms. A target the athlete values but does not believe in (a large testing jump, a return-to-play date) gets split into stages the athlete can see as reachable. A target the athlete can reach but does not value needs its outcome made worth something to that athlete. Eric's baseline: "New movement patterns are expected to take roughly 3-4 weeks of practice to become efficient" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 171, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: that expected timeline is one way to keep belief realistic when a new exercise is introduced, so early clumsiness is not read as failure.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors present the model without data, and the scales (-5 to +5, 0 to 1) are Vroom's as reported, not measured here. The page gives F as a single product and then as a sum over outcomes; both appear, for one goal and for a task with several outcomes. "Altering the athlete's perceptions" is not licence to inflate belief beyond the athlete's real capability; Inference: a target that is then missed lowers belief for the next one.

**Example** — The authors' own, in general form: a goal that is highly attractive but believed far out of reach yields little effort until it is broken into smaller goals matched to capability (PDF p. 353 / printed p. 342). Inference: an athlete told to add 100 kg to a squat over a year is given four quarterly targets instead.

# Situational Leadership for Coaches: Rate the Athlete's Maturity, Then Tell, Sell, Participate or Delegate

**What it is** — The model is Hersey and Blanchard's Situational Leadership Model, which the authors present for "the coach in playing a role as leader" (PDF p. 354 / printed p. 343, checked against the page image). "Hersey and Blanchard stated that leadership style ought to be implemented according to each situation which arises." Style is matched to the follower's "'maturity' (education, experience, responsibility, self-motivation, degree of self-actualization)."

Fig 6.19 (checked against the page image) plots relationship behaviour (vertical, low to high) against task behaviour (horizontal, low to high), with four quadrants: S1 Telling (high task, low relationship), S2 Selling (high task, high relationship), S3 Participating (low task, high relationship), S4 Delegating (low task, low relationship). A bell-shaped curve runs through them. Below the grid, maturity of followers runs M1 (low) at the high-task end to M4 (high) at the low-task end, so M1 pairs with S1 and M4 with S4.

How to use it: "the coach in playing a role as leader rates the maturity of the follower as low, moderate or high (M1, M2, M3 or M4), then reads off the appropriate leadership style (S1, S2, S3 or S4) in the relevant box above. Relationship behaviour includes the amount of time and effort put into interaction with followers. One spends more time in Selling or Participatory situations than in Telling or Delegating situations, hence the shape of the curve" (PDF p. 354 / printed p. 343).

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism or data beyond the model's logic: a follower low in experience and responsibility needs direction, and a mature one needs freedom. Inference: it is the coaching version of matching instruction to the learner.

**When to apply** — Deciding how much to direct an athlete, intern or staff member: a first-year athlete in a new lift gets Telling (clear instructions, little discussion); an experienced athlete who knows the method gets Participating or Delegating. Eric's baseline: interns "need both the 'why' (conceptual education) and the 'how' (hands-on technical training) each week" and should leave with "a professional portfolio of real work products" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 204, Explicit). Inference: that progression from instruction to owned work products is the M1-to-M4 path in this model.

**When NOT to apply** — The text says maturity is rated "low, moderate or high" but lists four levels (M1 to M4); the page does not say how the three words map to the four codes. The authors give no evidence that matching style to maturity improves results. Maturity is task-specific: Inference: the same athlete can be M4 in the squat and M1 in a new sprint drill, so rate per task, not per person.

**Example** — The authors give no worked case. Inference: a freshman lineman learning the hang clean gets S1 Telling from the coach; by his third year, running his own warm-up and accessory work within the plan, he gets S4 Delegating.

# Classify Sports by Movement Organisation and Energy Supply: Acyclic, Cyclic and Complex (Farfel 1969)

**What it is** — Programming rules need "the limits of generality and specificity in individual sports or groups of related sports," so sports must be classified "scientifically." "Classification of sports into individual, team, ball or water sports, for example, is not scientifically useful; it is more appropriate to classify sports on the basis of the particular organisation of the sporting movements and characteristics of the physical systems used to produce their working effect" (PDF p. 356 / printed p. 345, checked against the page image). The authors adopt three groups "as already outlined by Farfel (1969)" (PDF p. 357 / printed p. 346, checked against the page image):
1. **Acyclic sports**, "in which perfecting of the neuromuscular system for precise regulation of movements and the ability to produce great power play the dominant roles." Earlier on the same page: "complex organisation of motor actions and an intense concentration of working effort, displayed briefly," with energy "primarily through ATP-CP energy processes." Subgroups: "powerful, brief, explosive efforts" and "fine motor control and spatially precise movement."
2. **Cyclic sports** "(usually of submaximal and of moderate power), associated primarily with the production of muscular work through aerobic processes": "prolonged repetition of stereotyped work cycles of relatively simple organisation which do not require maximal muscular tension." Subgroups: "extensive oxygen utilisation" and work where "the muscles have an inadequate oxygen supply."
3. **Complex (combined) sports**, "where characteristically there is a high variability of motor actions under conditions of advancing fatigue and varying intensity of work, typified by team sports and one-on-one events (e.g. boxing and fencing)." Their energy production "is of a mixed aerobic-anaerobic character, with the greater part being derived from glycolytic reactions."

A second rule: "In classifying sports, it is necessary to consider competitive, as well as training activities," because training exercises can differ from competition, "often due to the necessity for repeated reproduction of the competitive movements in training"; this is where "special endurance (e.g. speed-, jumping-, and strength-endurance)" belongs. The authors' example: the 100 m takes about 10 s and "does not depend on oxidative efficiency. However, in order for a sprinter to prepare himself to effectively display such effort, he should execute training loads that develop his aerobic and anaerobic potential, in particular the latter" (PDF p. 357 / printed p. 346).

**Why it works** — The authors' rationale is physiological: "The more prolonged and the lower the intensity of muscular work, the greater the role of aerobic processes"; the glycolytic role "grows as the duration of work decreases and the power of muscular work increases"; in brief acyclic work under heavy load, athletes overcome resistance in "tenths and even hundredths of a second," which demands "an effective and reliable biodynamic structure" (PDF p. 356 / printed p. 345). Inference: the duration-intensity ordering of energy supply is standard exercise physiology; the three-group scheme itself is Farfel's convention, adopted without data, hence `supported` rather than `proven`.

**When to apply** — First question when writing a programme for a new sport or position: which group, and which subgroup? The authors use this scheme again in 6.8.2 to say which systems specialise (see Related). Eric's baseline: "A sport cannot maximize all three energy systems at once — priority has to be picked based on what the competition actually demands" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 115, Explicit). Inference: Farfel's grouping is a coarse first pass at that priority choice. The sprinter example supports training activities that differ from the competition's own energy profile.

**When NOT to apply** — Source against Eric's baseline on football: the authors put team sports in the complex group, with "the greater part" of energy "derived from glycolytic reactions" (PDF p. 357 / printed p. 346). Eric's baseline: for football, glycolytic conditioning "is treated as a 'worst case scenario' to be absorbed incidentally through camp and practice rather than programmed as a primary target" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 116, Explicit, claimed again in interview 2026-09-28, Q1), and "our staff does program it in the off-season" (line 117, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q19)). The authors give no football data, and "team sports" is a broad category. Inference: within the complex group, positions differ enough (a lineman's short bursts against a receiver's repeated sprints) that the group label decides little on its own; the authors' own call to "further subdivide" applies. This is a different scheme from Diachkov's four categories by motor regime used in 5.1 (see Related).

**Example** — The authors' own: boxing and fencing as one-on-one complex sports; the 100 m sprinter whose event does not depend on oxidative efficiency but whose training should still develop aerobic and, especially, anaerobic potential (PDF p. 357 / printed p. 346).

**Related** — [[framework--special-strength-methods-classified-by-sport-group-and-strength-type]] (Diachkov's four sport categories, 5.1; a different classification), [[principle--functional-specialisation-is-a-primary-emphasis-not-an-exclusive-energy-system]] (6.8.2 applies this scheme), [[heuristic--cyclic-vs-acyclic-speed-strength-tempo-rest-and-fatigue]], [[claim--energy-system-contribution-by-sport-table]], [[claim--all-round-athletes-main-regime-cyclic-and-phasic-tonic]]

# Classify Sports by Movement Organisation and Energy Supply: Acyclic, Cyclic and Complex (Farfel 1969)

**What it is** — Programming rules need "the limits of generality and specificity in individual sports or groups of related sports," so sports must be classified "scientifically." "Classification of sports into individual, team, ball or water sports, for example, is not scientifically useful; it is more appropriate to classify sports on the basis of the particular organisation of the sporting movements and characteristics of the physical systems used to produce their working effect" (PDF p. 356 / printed p. 345, checked against the page image). The authors adopt three groups "as already outlined by Farfel (1969)" (PDF p. 357 / printed p. 346, checked against the page image):
1. **Acyclic sports**, "in which perfecting of the neuromuscular system for precise regulation of movements and the ability to produce great power play the dominant roles." Earlier on the same page: "complex organisation of motor actions and an intense concentration of working effort, displayed briefly," with energy "primarily through ATP-CP energy processes." Subgroups: "powerful, brief, explosive efforts" and "fine motor control and spatially precise movement."
2. **Cyclic sports** "(usually of submaximal and of moderate power), associated primarily with the production of muscular work through aerobic processes": "prolonged repetition of stereotyped work cycles of relatively simple organisation which do not require maximal muscular tension." Subgroups: "extensive oxygen utilisation" and work where "the muscles have an inadequate oxygen supply."
3. **Complex (combined) sports**, "where characteristically there is a high variability of motor actions under conditions of advancing fatigue and varying intensity of work, typified by team sports and one-on-one events (e.g. boxing and fencing)." Their energy production "is of a mixed aerobic-anaerobic character, with the greater part being derived from glycolytic reactions."

A second rule: "In classifying sports, it is necessary to consider competitive, as well as training activities," because training exercises can differ from competition, "often due to the necessity for repeated reproduction of the competitive movements in training"; this is where "special endurance (e.g. speed-, jumping-, and strength-endurance)" belongs. The authors' example: the 100 m takes about 10 s and "does not depend on oxidative efficiency. However, in order for a sprinter to prepare himself to effectively display such effort, he should execute training loads that develop his aerobic and anaerobic potential, in particular the latter" (PDF p. 357 / printed p. 346).

**Why it works** — The authors' rationale is physiological: "The more prolonged and the lower the intensity of muscular work, the greater the role of aerobic processes"; the glycolytic role "grows as the duration of work decreases and the power of muscular work increases"; in brief acyclic work under heavy load, athletes overcome resistance in "tenths and even hundredths of a second," which demands "an effective and reliable biodynamic structure" (PDF p. 356 / printed p. 345). # Plan in Mesocycles, Not Microcycles, and Do Not Read Every Planned Dip in Work Capacity as a Programming Error

**What it is** — The authors list three practical rules that followed from supercompensation research (Weigert's law, "first formally described by Folbrot (1941, 1952, 1958)"; also Yakovlev 1955, 1975; Gorkin et al 1973; Volkov 1975; Monogarov & Platonov 1975; Sergeyev 1981) (PDF p. 358 / printed p. 347, checked against the page image):
- "It is necessary for the athlete to maintain a state of adaptation during training, so that it is possible to execute the fundamental sporting actions effectively over an extended period"
- "Repetition of training loads when the body is in a state of insufficient restoration is generally undesirable, although this is permissible in certain instances"
- "Special work capacity should rise steadily during the course of training; any decrease at given stages of training would indicate that the training is incorrectly organised."

Their verdict: "Undoubtedly, all of these premises were progressive in their time and to a certain extent are still valid today. However, modern sporting requirements reveal the necessity to alter the main approach to structuring training and obey common sense, which indicates that the fundamental unit of training should be the mesocycle and not the microcycle." This requires "An extensive study of the characteristics of long-term adaptation," whose value "will be appreciated only if one can observe the specific effect of given training loads on the dynamics of the athlete's state and determine the quantitative characteristics of the adaptation process" (PDF p. 358 / printed p. 347).

The same section then describes a loading form that deliberately lowers the functional indicators for weeks (concentrated loading, Fig 6.23; PDF pp. 360-361 / printed pp. 349-350). Inference: this is the authors' own revision of the third rule: a planned decrease inside a concentrated mesocycle is not, in their model, a sign of incorrect organisation.

**Why it works** — The authors' reason is that the effects they care about (long-term adaptation, delayed gains after concentrated loading) unfold over weeks, so judging each microcycle against the previous one misreads them. They give no study for the mesocycle claim itself on this page; "common sense" is their stated basis.

**When to apply** — Reviewing a plan: judge progress block by block, not week by week, especially during a deliberately heavy block. Eric's baseline: "Weekly tracking is preferred over infrequent (e.g., once-a-phase) testing, specifically to catch plateaus or declines early enough to adjust programming" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 59, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the two fit if weekly data are read against the mesocycle's expected shape: a decline during a planned concentrated block is expected, while the same decline in a normal block is a signal. Eric's baseline: undulating periodization, "waving volume week to week" (line 106, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: a wave inside a mesocycle is already a planned non-steady rise.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors keep the old rules "to a certain extent ... still valid," and the second one ("generally undesirable ... permissible in certain instances") is not withdrawn. Inference: a decline outside a planned loading block, or one that does not recover when load drops, is still the warning the third rule describes. Batch 6a (sections 6.1 to 6.3, Matveyev's periodisation and "The Periodisation Controversy," PDF pp. 324-346) may carry an overlapping entry on the authors' critique of classical periodisation; this entry is limited to the 6.8.1 statement.

**Example** — The authors' own contrast: the third rule says any decrease means the training is "incorrectly organised" (PDF p. 358 / printed p. 347), while concentrated loading produces a "decrease of the functional indicators" followed by a rise that "exceeds the level achieved with the first form of adaptation" (PDF p. 360 / printed p. 349).

**What it is** — From "observing the dynamics of an athlete's special physical preparedness indicators over many years of training," the authors state four conclusions, mainly for "sports which require explosive effort" (PDF p. 358 / printed p. 347, checked against the page image):
1. "The absolute and mean level of special strength preparedness increases annually."
2. "The initial level of speed-strength in each annual cycle is lower than the level at the end of the preceding year's, but higher than at its beginning."
3. "The rise in speed-strength from year to year is larger for athletes of medium qualification than for highly qualified athletes."
4. The annual trend "is determined by the traditional periodisation of training for the given sport and competition calendar. One can clearly trace a twin peak in the dynamics of speed-strength with two competition stages, because the level of special strength preparedness is higher in the second competition stage than in the first. In types of sports with one competition season, speed-strength rises regularly and uniformly."

The text assigns B to bi-cyclic and C to mono-cyclic periodisation, and A to "relatively stable, long-term adaptation over many years." Inference: for an athlete whose speed-strength has plateaued across years, conclusion 1 no longer describes them; that is the limit the parabola refers to.
