# Compensatory Adaptation Is Temporary and Comes First; Stable Adaptation Builds on It, and Has a Limit

**What it is** — The authors split adaptation into two layers (PDF p. 359 / printed p. 348; text layer only for this page, the figure it refers to was checked on PDF p. 358):
- **Compensatory adaptation.** The annual changes in functional indicators (Fig 6.22, graphs B and C) "are temporary, unstable and to a certain extent, reversible." Their basis is "compensatory mechanisms, i.e. reactions designed to maintain the necessary level of functioning for brief periods under demanding conditions which ultimately lead to stable adaptation." These "gradually fade as adaptation takes place," and "Insofar as these mechanisms precede adaptation, they should be designated pre-adaptation phenomena (Kuznyetsov, 1979)."
- **Long-term, stable adaptation** (graph A). "compensatory adaptation is a prerequisite condition for the development of long-term, stable adaptation," which "can progressively increase if the functional reconstruction during the course of compensatory adaptation is sufficient to produce a noticeable effect on the external interactions of the body and increase its special work capacity."

Three further statements on the same page:
1. "adaptation cannot be considered an equilibrium process. Adaptation is the dynamic maintenance of a definite level of imbalance between the body and the environment" (Bauer, 1935; Bernstein, 1966).
2. The systems involved improve at different rates. This heterochronicity "is determined by: the action of particular physiological systems in establishing long-term adaptation of a specific emphasis; differences in their reactiveness (or adaptive inertia); changes in the role of these systems at different stages of long-term adaptation."
3. "Long-term compensatory adaptation cannot continue indefinitely." Its effect "diminishes with each repetition," described "by a parabola whose peak is eventually reached with time (Fig 6.22, graph A). This indicates that an athlete's general adaptation reserves have a limit that is genetically predetermined." The limit shows as "waves in the dynamics of special work capacity (graphs B and C)," caused partly by "traditional periodisation" but "a more important reason is the exhaustion of the so-called current adaptation reserves (CAR) of the body."

**Why it works** — The authors' account is the one above: short-term compensations hold function under stress, and if they change performance enough, the body consolidates them. They state that the picture is clearest in explosive-strength sports and that endurance adaptation "has to be taken much further," assuming "the same, above-mentioned chief mechanisms, although at another level of the physiological systems" (PDF p. 359 / printed p. 348). The "genetically predetermined" limit is inferred from the shape of the curve, not from genetic data.

**When to apply** — Inference: treat a season's gains in functional indicators as provisional until they hold through a lower-load period; a quality that survives the transition phase has become stable adaptation in the authors' terms. When a block stops producing gains, the authors' model points to exhausted current reserves before it points to a genetic ceiling (see [[principle--load-must-sit-within-the-current-adaptation-reserve-window]]).

**When NOT to apply** — Page 359 was read from the text layer only. No data are given for the parabola or the genetic limit, and Fig 6.22's graph A looks nearly straight over the three years drawn, not parabolic. The "imbalance" definition is a theoretical position (Bauer, Bernstein), not a measured one. Inference: it sits closer to the allostasis view than to classical homeostasis; see the Evans entry in Related.

**Example** — The authors' own: Fig 6.22, where the functional indicators B and C wave above and below the steadily rising fitness state A within each year (PDF p. 358 / printed p. 347).

# Load Must Sit Inside the Current Adaptation Reserve Window: Too Little Wastes It, Too Much Exhausts It

**What it is** — The authors make the current adaptation reserves (CAR) a programming rule (PDF p. 359 / printed p. 348, text layer only): "At any instant, the body has a definite reserve potential, i.e. a capability of responding to adapt to external influences and raise itself to a new functional level," limited by "definite physiological mechanisms." Hence "the intensity, volume and duration of the training influences determine the optimal development of the body's CAR. If the magnitude of these are below certain thresholds, the body will not fully utilise its CAR, whereas, if they exceed it, exhaustion of reserve potential will occur and the training effect will be low or negative."

The goal follows: "one can consider training organisation to be effective when it produces the maximum growth of the body's CAR by means of the appropriate volume of loading." Useful programming therefore needs "means of assessing the body's CAR in each case, together with criteria for determining the contents and volume of the training loads," and a quantitative approach "is based, in particular, on assessments of a number of bio-chemical indicators of energy exchange processes (Beckman et al, 1961; Yakovlev, 1977)" (PDF p. 360 / printed p. 349, checked against the page image).

The authors place this inside the older three-phase schemes of form: "(a) the growth of trainability, (b) sporting form, (c) loss of trainability (Letunov, 1952)"; "(a) adaptation, (b) the highest sport work-capacity, (c) re-adaptation (Prokor, 1959)," where re-adaptation is "decrease in work capacity as the limits of adaptability are exceeded" (PDF pp. 359-360 / printed pp. 348-349); and Matveyev's "acquisition, preservation and brief loss of sporting form (Matveyev, 1964)" (PDF p. 360 / printed p. 349). "Prokor" is the book's spelling.

**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning is a threshold model: a reserve with a fixed size at any moment is under-used by small loads and depleted by large ones. They give no measured threshold. Inference: this is the same inverted-U logic as the dose-response models elsewhere in the library, applied to a whole training phase.

**When to apply** — Inference: when a block produces no gain, ask first whether the load was below threshold (too little) or beyond it (exhaustion); the remedy is opposite in the two cases. The authors' wave signal (see Related) is one way to tell: waves in special work capacity mark the reserve running out. Eric's baseline: the mRSI decision read uses individualized thresholds, "Percent change from baseline or a rolling average. We've used standard deviations and SWC to diagnose signal versus noise" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 75, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q2, Q2a)). **What it is** — The authors make the current adaptation reserves (CAR) a programming rule (PDF p. 359 / printed p. 348, text layer only): "At any instant, the body has a definite reserve potential, i.e. a capability of responding to adapt to external influences and raise itself to a new functional level," limited by "definite physiological mechanisms." Hence "the intensity, volume and duration of the training influences determine the optimal development of the body's CAR. If the magnitude of these are below certain thresholds, the body will not fully utilise its CAR, whereas, if they exceed it, exhaustion of reserve potential will occur and the training effect will be low or negative."

The goal follows: "one can consider training organisation to be effective when it produces the maximum growth of the body's CAR by means of the appropriate volume of loading." Useful programming therefore needs "means of assessing the body's CAR in each case, together with criteria for determining the contents and volume of the training loads," and a quantitative approach "is based, in particular, on assessments of a number of bio-chemical indicators of energy exchange processes (Beckman et al, 1961; Yakovlev, 1977)" (PDF p. 360 / printed p. 349, checked against the page image).

"Prokor" is the book's spelling.

# Two Forms of Compensatory Adaptation: Distributed Loading Rises Gradually; Concentrated Loading Dips First, Then Rises Higher

**What it is** — "Two forms of compensatory adaptation, associated with enhancing the CAR by systematic training, which differ in volume and organisation of the training loads, have been identified and studied in explosive sports" (PDF p. 360 / printed p. 349, checked against the page image):
- **(A) Distributed loading:** "a gradual increase in the functional indicators," with "a moderate volume of continuous loading." "periodic brief disturbances of the body's homeostasis occur and the current expenditure of energy resources is compensated during training." It "follows traditional concepts for developing trainability and is typical for athletes of medium classification."
- **(B) Concentrated loading:** "a large, concentrated volume of special physical preparation means, concentrated in the first half of the training phase. These large volumes provoke a profound and prolonged disturbance of the body's homeostasis, which is reflected by decrease of the functional indicators. Then, after the volume of loading is decreased, their increase accelerates and exceeds the level achieved with the first form of adaptation. This way of organising loading in the preparatory mesocycles was devised for highly qualified athletes and has been shown by research to be effective for all types of sport (Verkhoshansky, 1977)."

Fig 6.23, "Two forms of compensatory adaptation during the large preparation phase (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999)" (PDF p. 361 / printed p. 350, checked against the page image and high-resolution crops of both panels), plots % change (100 = start) over 18 weeks, with dashed lines at weeks 6 and 12. Values read by eye, all "about":
- **Panel A (distributed):** every curve rises from week 0. At week 18, starting strength about 144%, explosive strength about 128%; the three lower curves end at about 114%, 108% and 105%, matching the right-hand labels maximum strength, absolute strength and speed by end position. By that reading, speed peaks at about 113% near week 9 and then declines.
- **Panel B (concentrated):** every curve falls first, to lows between about 83% and about 96% around weeks 4-6, crosses back above 100% around weeks 7-9, and ends at week 18 at about 157% (starting strength), 143% (explosive strength), 129% (maximum strength, after a peak of about 131% near week 16), 120% (speed) and 114% (absolute strength). The page does not let one tell which quality dips deepest.

The authors' further claim: "the more extensive and longer the exhaustion of the body's energy resources by concentrated loading during specific mesocycles of training (obviously within reasonable limits), the higher their subsequent super-restoration and the longer the new functional level is maintained" (Verkhoshansky, 1977). "The key issue, of course, is determining the optimal duration of concentrated loading, so as to avoid exhaustion and diminished performance" (PDF pp. 360-361 / printed pp. 349-350).

On critics: Komarova (1984) "correctly recognises that premature or prolonged application of concentrated loading can lead to overtraining, stagnation or injury," but "errs in extrapolating this analysis to completely dismiss the periodic use of concentrated loading by qualified athletes" (PDF p. 360 / printed p. 349).

**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism is the compensatory sequence: a large, prolonged homeostatic disturbance depresses function, and when volume drops the compensatory reaction overshoots. They cite Verkhoshansky (1977) and give no sample or data beyond Fig 6.23, which carries no study label.

**When to apply** — Inference: concentrated loading is the authors' choice for highly qualified athletes in preparatory mesocycles with time to absorb a dip of several weeks; distributed loading for medium-level athletes or when performance must hold. Eric's baseline: "Off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first; already-strong athletes shift more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds "Not claimed in the interview"). Inference: the authors' split by qualification sits alongside that baseline split by strength level.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested across the library:** the authors say concentrated loading "has been shown by research to be effective for all types of sport" (PDF p. 360 / printed p. 349). Issurin (2016) judged the concentrated-unidirectional evidence insufficient for broad use in high-performance combat, team-sport and swimming preparation, noting fitness gains without reported effects on team practice or competition (p. 6), and placed the model as better suited to sports dominated by a narrow target quality (p. 11) ([[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]). Figure against text: the figure's depressed phase (below 100% until about weeks 7-9) runs longer than the 3-4 week concentrated block the authors give on the same page, and its x-axis ends at 18 weeks while the text's period is 18-22 weeks (see [[heuristic--concentrated-blocks-of-3-4-weeks-three-in-a-row-then-longer-recovery]]). Inference: the "deeper exhaustion, higher rebound" claim sits on the same pages as the Bondarchuk result the authors read as "calculations of volume are not as critical as those of intensity" (PDF p. 361 / printed p. 350); the authors do not reconcile the two (see [[claim--bondarchuk-50-percent-more-volume-did-not-prolong-training-effect]]). Not for novices or medium-level athletes, by the authors' own scope.

**Example** — The authors' own: Fig 6.23, where after concentrated loading starting strength ends at about 157% against about 144% with distributed loading over the same 18 weeks (PDF p. 361 / printed p. 350).

# Two Forms of Compensatory Adaptation: Distributed Loading Rises Gradually; Concentrated Loading Dips First, Then Rises Higher

**What it is** — "Two forms of compensatory adaptation, associated with enhancing the CAR by systematic training, which differ in volume and organisation of the training loads, have been identified and studied in explosive sports" (PDF p. 360 / printed p. 349, checked against the page image):
- **(A) Distributed loading:** "a gradual increase in the functional indicators," with "a moderate volume of continuous loading." "periodic brief disturbances of the body's homeostasis occur and the current expenditure of energy resources is compensated during training." It "follows traditional concepts for developing trainability and is typical for athletes of medium classification."
- **(B) Concentrated loading:** "a large, concentrated volume of special physical preparation means, concentrated in the first half of the training phase. These large volumes provoke a profound and prolonged disturbance of the body's homeostasis, which is reflected by decrease of the functional indicators. Then, after the volume of loading is decreased, their increase accelerates and exceeds the level achieved with the first form of adaptation. This way of organising loading in the preparatory mesocycles was devised for highly qualified athletes and has been shown by research to be effective for all types of sport (Verkhoshansky, 1977)."

Fig 6.23, "Two forms of compensatory adaptation during the large preparation phase (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999)" (PDF p. 361 / printed p. 350, checked against the page image and high-resolution crops of both panels), plots % change (100 = start) over 18 weeks, with dashed lines at weeks 6 and 12. Values read by eye, all "about":
- **Panel A (distributed):** every curve rises from week 0. At week 18, starting strength about 144%, explosive strength about 128%; the three lower curves end at about 114%, 108% and 105%, matching the right-hand labels maximum strength, absolute strength and speed by end position. By that reading, speed peaks at about 113% near week 9 and then declines.
- **Panel B (concentrated):** every curve falls first, to lows between about 83% and about 96% around weeks 4-6, crosses back above 100% around weeks 7-9, and ends at week 18 at about 157% (starting strength), 143% (explosive strength), 129% (maximum strength, after a peak of about 131% near week 16), 120% (speed) and 114% (absolute strength). The page does not let one tell which quality dips deepest.

The authors' further claim: "the more extensive and longer the exhaustion of the body's energy resources by concentrated loading during specific mesocycles of training (obviously within reasonable limits), the higher their subsequent super-restoration and the longer the new functional level is maintained" (Verkhoshansky, 1977). "The key issue, of course, is determining the optimal duration of concentrated loading, so as to avoid exhaustion and diminished performance" (PDF pp. 360-361 / printed pp. 349-350).

On critics: Komarova (1984) "correctly recognises that premature or prolonged application of concentrated loading can lead to overtraining, stagnation or injury," but "errs in extrapolating this analysis to completely dismiss the periodic use of concentrated loading by qualified athletes" (PDF p. 360 / printed p. 349).

**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism is the compensatory sequence: a large, prolonged homeostatic disturbance depresses function, and when volume drops the compensatory reaction overshoots. They cite Verkhoshansky (1977) and give no sample or data beyond Fig 6.23, which carries no study label.

**When to apply** — Inference: concentrated loading is the authors' choice for highly qualified athletes in preparatory mesocycles with time to absorb a dip of several weeks; distributed loading for medium-level athletes or when performance must hold. Eric's baseline: "Off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first; already-strong athletes shift more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds "Not claimed in the interview"). Inference: the authors' split by qualification sits alongside that baseline split by strength level.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested across the library:** the authors say concentrated loading "has been shown by research to be effective for all types of sport" (PDF p. 360 / printed p. 349). Issurin (2016) judged the concentrated-unidirectional evidence insufficient for broad use in high-performance combat, team-sport and swimming preparation, noting fitness gains without reported effects on team practice or competition (p. 6), and placed the model as better suited to sports dominated by a narrow target quality (p. 11) ([[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]). Figure against text: the figure's depressed phase (below 100% until about weeks 7-9) runs longer than the 3-4 week concentrated block the authors give on the same page, and its x-axis ends at 18 weeks while the text's period is 18-22 weeks (see [[heuristic--concentrated-blocks-of-3-4-weeks-three-in-a-row-then-longer-recovery]]). Inference: the "deeper exhaustion, higher rebound" claim sits on the same pages as the Bondarchuk result the authors read as "calculations of volume are not as critical as those of intensity" (PDF p. 361 / printed p. 350); the authors do not reconcile the two (see [[claim--bondarchuk-50-percent-more-volume-did-not-prolong-training-effect]]). Not for novices or medium-level athletes, by the authors' own scope.

**Example** — The authors' own: Fig 6.23, where after concentrated loading starting strength ends at about 157% against about 144% with distributed loading over the same 18 weeks (PDF p. 361 / printed p. 350).

# Block Durations for Enhancing the Adaptation Reserve: 5-6 Weeks Continuous or 3-4 Weeks Concentrated, Three Blocks With 7-10 Day Pauses, Then a Longer Recovery

**What it is** — The authors give the durations "vital for maximal enhancement of the body's CAR" (PDF p. 360 / printed p. 349, checked against the page image):
1. "the appropriate duration of continuous training is 5-6 weeks, and with concentrated loading, the duration is 3-4 weeks, after which a recuperation period is necessary for activating the compensatory processes."
2. "the trained athlete is able to tolerate three such sequential blocks of loading, separated by short recuperation pauses (7-10 days). After this, a longer recuperation period is necessary to facilitate stabilisation at the new level of adaptation."
3. "Thus, the time interval necessary for exhausting the body's CAR is between 18-22 weeks (see Fig 6.23). This period coincides with observations of highly qualified athletes training in different sports, including cyclic types (Zhikharevich, 1976; Sirenko, 1980)."
4. "the body cannot indefinitely continue to adapt successively to training loads," and "it is inappropriate to subject the body to extreme exhaustion of its energy reserves. This requires a longer recuperation period and has a negative effect on the subsequent stages of adaptation."

**Why it works** — The authors' reason is the CAR model: each block draws on a limited reserve, the recuperation pause lets the compensatory reaction occur, and after about three blocks the reserve is spent (see [[principle--load-must-sit-within-the-current-adaptation-reserve-window]]). No data for the durations are shown beyond the two citations for the 18-22 week period.

**When to apply** — Inference: sketching an off-season or preparatory phase for a trained athlete: up to three loading blocks, each followed by a 7-10 day lighter pause, then a longer recovery before the next phase. Eric's baseline: "An annual plan is treated as a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 183, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the 18-22 week ceiling is a reason to place a longer recovery period on that roadmap rather than run loading blocks back to back.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested inside the book (concentrated block duration).** Here a concentrated block lasts "3-4 weeks, after which a recuperation period is necessary" (PDF p. 360 / printed p. 349). In 5.3.3 the book says "unidirectional training over periods as long as 4-12 weeks can be very effective" and refers to "4-8 week concentrated blocks of strength, speed-strength or speed training" (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294; wording confirmed in the text layer, and verified against the image in [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]]). Inference: one reading reconciles them (three 3-4 week blocks give about 9-12 weeks of unidirectional emphasis), but the book does not say so. **Unclear arithmetic:** three 5-6 week continuous blocks plus two 7-10 day pauses come to about 17-21 weeks; three 3-4 week concentrated blocks plus two pauses come to about 11-15 weeks. The text does not say which form the 18-22 weeks refers to, and Fig 6.23, which it cites, spans only 18 weeks. Inference: the 18-22 week figure fits the continuous form better. The authors do not say how the pause length or the "longer recuperation period" should be set beyond these figures.

**Example** — The authors give the rule, not a worked plan. Inference: a January-to-May preparatory phase of three 4-week concentrated blocks, each followed by a 7-10 day lighter week, then a two- to three-week recovery period before summer training.

**Related** — [[framework--distributed-vs-concentrated-loading-two-forms-of-compensatory-adaptation]], [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]], [[heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]], [[heuristic--restorative-stage-length-scales-with-homeostatic-disturbance]], [[principle--load-must-sit-within-the-current-adaptation-reserve-window]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--accumulation-mesocycle-duration-and-monitoring]] (Issurin: accumulation blocks up to about six weeks, with gains falling sharply after that), [[block-periodization--issurin/case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]] (Bondarchuk's four-week blocks with two-week restorative blocks)

# After Heavy Disturbance, Cut Total Volume and Add General Physical Preparation; the Deeper the Disturbance, the Longer the Restorative Stage

**What it is** — The authors' rule for restorative stages after concentrated loading (PDF p. 361 / printed p. 350, checked against the page image): "Training organisation which elicits extensive and relatively prolonged disturbance of homeostasis necessitates the inclusion of suitable restorative stages for triggering a compensatory reaction, thereby eliminating inappropriately phased peaking of the various functional indicators and stabilising the body at the new functional level. The general volume of the load should be decreased at this time and General Physical Preparation means should be introduced into training so as to intensify the compensatory reaction. The more extensive and prolonged the disturbance of homeostasis, the longer the restorative stage should be."

Three parts:
1. **Purpose:** trigger the compensatory reaction, prevent the functional indicators from peaking out of phase with each other, and stabilise the new level.
2. **Content:** lower total volume, and bring in General Physical Preparation (GPP) means.
3. **Length:** scaled to the size and duration of the preceding disturbance.

**Why it works** — The authors' reason is the compensatory model: the gains of a concentrated block appear only after volume falls ("after the volume of loading is decreased, their increase accelerates"; PDF p. 360 / printed p. 349). They do not say why GPP intensifies the reaction, and give no data for it.

**When to apply** — Inference: plan the stage after any deliberately heavy block as a change of content, not only a cut in load: lower volume of special means, more general work. Inference: size its length to the block before it, longer after a longer or heavier block. Eric's baseline: "Recovery capacity must be 'earned' by training hard enough first" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 151, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the authors' rule is the other half of that statement: once the hard block has been done, the restorative stage is part of the plan.

**When NOT to apply** — No durations are given for the restorative stage here. Inference: "GPP" here is not defined; the means chosen should still not undo the quality just built.

# Bondarchuk (1982): 50% More Volume of the Same Programme Did Not Lengthen the Training Effect in Hammer Throwers

**What it is** — The authors report: "a study done by Bondarchuk (1982) which analysed the effect of different volumes of an identical training programme on a group of hammer-throwers. He found that a 50% increase in volume of loading had no significant effect on the duration of maintenance of the training effect and sporting performance. Although Bondarchuk stresses that this finding applies strictly to a particular group of athletes, it tends to confirm that major changes in intensity have a more profound effect on athletic state than comparable changes in volume. It also implies that calculations of volume are not as critical as those of intensity, thus corroborating the importance of paying careful attention to zones of loading intensity, as emphasized earlier in 6.2.2 (see also Table 6.1)" (PDF p. 361 / printed p. 350, checked against the page image; the last phrase is italic in the original).

Two layers: Bondarchuk's finding (50% more volume, no significant change in how long the training effect and performance were maintained) and the authors' extrapolation (intensity matters more than volume).

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's study as reported does not test intensity at all; the comparison with intensity is the authors' reading. No sample size, volumes, durations or measures are given on the page.

**When to apply** — Inference: as one reason not to answer a stalled thrower or strength athlete with more of the same work. Eric's baseline: "In-season, the stated rule is 'maintain intensity, reduce volume'" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds "Not claimed in the interview"). Inference: the Bondarchuk result is consistent with that rule's premise that volume can drop without losing the effect, though it was not an in-season study.

**When NOT to apply** — One group of hammer throwers, by Bondarchuk's own caveat "strictly" limited to them; hence `untested`. The study varied volume only, so "intensity has a more profound effect" is not shown by it. Inference: on the page before, the authors argue the opposite direction for volume: "the more extensive and longer the exhaustion of the body's energy resources by concentrated loading ... the higher their subsequent super-restoration and the longer the new functional level is maintained" (PDF p. 360 / printed p. 349), which makes concentrated volume the lever; the authors set the two side by side without reconciling them. The Table 6.1 and 6.2.2 material it points to is in batch 6a's pages (PDF pp. 334-336), not checked here.

**Example** — The authors' own: Bondarchuk's hammer throwers, whose 50% volume increase did not change how long the training effect was maintained (PDF p. 361 / printed p. 350).

# Specialisation Sets a Primary Emphasis, Not an Exclusive System: Explosive Athletes Need Aerobic Efficiency, Endurance Athletes Need Strength

**What it is** — "Structural-functional specialisation refers to those stable, adaptive changes that are produced by the specific form of conditioning imposed by a given sport," and "those systems which are of major importance for success in sport undergo an accelerated rate of functional growth" (PDF p. 361 / printed p. 350, checked against the page image). The specifics of adaptation are set by "the work regime in sports, and the gradual, but steady increase in complexity of the body's external interactions associated with the growth of sporting proficiency" (PDF p. 362 / printed p. 351, checked against the page image).

Using the sport groups, "specialisation by physiological system means that acyclic sports rely predominantly on anaerobic processes and functional hypertrophy of the motor apparatus, whereas cyclic sports place major reliance on aerobic processes. In complex (combined) sports, there is an intense functional development of both the motor apparatus and the energy production systems" (PDF p. 362 / printed p. 351). The page says "the classification scheme of 6.5"; the scheme is in 6.7.

The new point is the qualifier: "specialisation in the first two cases does not imply that development is either strictly aerobic or anaerobic, but rather that there is a particular primary emphasis of functional specialisation. One can successfully develop a high level of explosive strength in acyclic locomotion only when one possesses sufficiently high aerobic efficiency. At the same time, improving the efficiency of the energy producing systems in cyclic locomotion should be based on highly developed muscular strength and local muscular endurance" (PDF p. 362 / printed p. 351). For cyclic sports: "strength preparedness, mainly in the form of strength-endurance, plays an important role" (Zhurbinoi, 1978).

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for why explosive strength needs aerobic efficiency on this page. For the cyclic side they point to Chapter 4's argument that endurance rests on muscular as well as respiratory qualities (see Related). On cost they add: "energy expenditure being almost proportional to the fourth power of running speed (Sargent, 1926)," with the rising cost met by "a greater reliance being placed on anaerobic processes" (Henry, 1951; Margaria, 1963) (PDF p. 362 / printed p. 351). The fourth-power figure carries only that 1926 citation, and no later check is given.

**When to apply** — Inference: when a speed-power programme drops all aerobic work, or an endurance programme drops strength work, this principle argues for keeping a supporting dose of the other. Eric's baseline: "For speed-power athletes, the aerobic system's main value is inter-effort recovery (regenerating ATP between bouts)" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 123, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: that is one plausible route for the authors' "sufficiently high aerobic efficiency," though the authors do not give it. Eric's baseline: football's priority stack names "alactic and aerobic capacity/power" as Goals 1 and 2 (line 116, Explicit, claimed again in interview 2026-09-28, Q1). Inference: the baseline already pairs the explosive and aerobic systems, as the authors' qualifier does.

**When NOT to apply** — "Sufficiently high" is not quantified, and no study is cited for the acyclic half of the claim. Inference: it does not license large aerobic volumes for power athletes; the claim is a minimum, not a target. The heterochronicity point on the same page ("the body adapts to external influences only when they become necessary for the further growth of sporting proficiency") is already covered by the Chapter 2 heterochronicity entry in Related and is not re-atomized here.

**Example** — The authors' own: improving the triple jump "requires developing the ability of the motor apparatus to produce great power," and a longer jump, gained mainly through running speed, brings "a significant increase in complexity of the interaction of the feet with the support at each take-off, a situation that requires significant improvement in reactive ability" (PDF p. 362 / printed p. 351).

**Related** — [[framework--three-sport-groups-acyclic-cyclic-complex-for-programming]], [[framework--specific-correspondence-of-the-training-effect-four-tasks]] (5.4.3, specialisation by system and by ability), [[framework--four-level-functional-specialisation-and-special-physical-preparedness]], [[claim--endurance-rests-on-muscle-oxidative-and-strength-qualities-not-vo2max]], [[principle--motor-system-leads-cardiorespiratory-adaptation-do-not-separate-them]], [[claim--heterochronicity-of-strength-quality-and-muscle-group-development-order]], [[claim--sprint-and-distance-training-emphasis-shifts-with-qualification-vankov]]

# Training Emphasis Shifts With Qualification: Sprinters Move From Aerobic Endurance and Speed to Speed Endurance; Distance Runners Add Anaerobic Work at the Top (Vankov 1978)

**What it is** — The authors report Vankov (1978) on multi-year emphasis (PDF p. 362 / printed p. 351, checked against the page image): "In the multi-year training of sprinters, up to Class I-CMS (Class I - Candidate for Master of Sport), the chief emphasis is on developing general (aerobic) endurance and speed, whereas at MS-MSIC (Master of Sport - Master of Sport, International Class) level the emphasis is on developing speed (anaerobic) endurance. In the training of distance athletes of all qualification levels, the chief emphasis is on developing aerobic productivity, while at the MS-MSIC level, the emphasis is on enhancing anaerobic productivity (Vankov, 1978)."

The surrounding point: kinesiological patterns across sports "are approximately equivalent, although there are some qualitative and quantitative differences"; "sprint swimmers have higher rates and developmental levels of anaerobic productivity than distance swimmers, whereas aerobic productivity is superior for distance swimmers. This is determined by the emphasis of the training" (PDF p. 362 / printed p. 351).

**Why it works** — The authors attribute the swimmer differences to training emphasis; no mechanism is given for the qualification shift. Inference: it fits the convergence principle, in which training effects move toward the sport's specific regime as mastery rises (see Related).

**When to apply** — Inference: in long-term plans for sprinters, a broad aerobic and speed base below national-class level, with speed endurance becoming the main emphasis only at the top. Eric's baseline: "The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill, each level a required foundation for the next)" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 101, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: Vankov's sprinter sequence also starts from general capacity and narrows toward the event's specific demand.

**When NOT to apply** — **Unclear as printed.** The distance-runner sentence says the chief emphasis is aerobic "of all qualification levels" and then that "at the MS-MSIC level, the emphasis is on enhancing anaerobic productivity," which contradicts "all." Inference: the likely meaning is that aerobic work stays the chief emphasis at every level and anaerobic work is added at the top, but the page does not say so. Soviet classification levels (Class I, CMS, MS, MSIC) do not map directly onto college levels, and no data, sample or event distances are given; hence `supported` at most.

**Example** — The authors' own: sprint swimmers with higher anaerobic and distance swimmers with higher aerobic productivity, "determined by the emphasis of the training" (PDF p. 362 / printed p. 351).

**Related** — [[principle--functional-specialisation-is-a-primary-emphasis-not-an-exclusive-energy-system]], [[principle--converging-partial-effects-of-strength-training-means]], [[claim--russian-sport-school-age-guidelines-table]], [[claim--four-observations-on-long-term-speed-strength-adaptation]], [[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/claim--endurance-event-transfer-range-widens-with-distance]]

+# Sirenko (1980): Same Running, Two Concentrated Strength Peaks Instead of One, Better 800 m and 1500 m Gains

+**What it is** — To show that a runner's aerobic and anaerobic state "depends on the contents and organisation of the training loads," the authors report Sirenko (1980): two groups of middle-distance runners over an annual cycle, each with "the same volume and distribution of running means," but "Group 1 used a traditional single-peak distribution of strength-means, whereas Group 2 used a double-peaked distribution of means with the emphasis concentrated in December and March-April" (PDF p. 378 / printed p. 367, checked against the page image). "Group 2 proved superior in all tests of functional ability, including aerobic efficiency, 'anaerobic threshold' (onset of blood lactate accumulation) and the results of control runs of 400m and 1200m, as well as in their sporting performances. During the summer competition stage Group 2 improved the 800m time by an average of 4.8 seconds and the 1500m run by 6.3 seconds, whereas in Group 1, the improvements were 3.4 and 4.6 seconds, respectively" (same page).

+**Why it works** — The authors present the study as evidence that content and organisation, not running volume alone, set the fitness state; they give no mechanism for why two concentrated strength peaks beat one. Inference: it fits their account of concentrated loading and the delayed rise that follows it ([[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]), and the LDTE of concentrated strength loading in middle-distance runners that they report from Zhdanovich (1980) on PDF p. 374.

+**When to apply** — Planning strength work for endurance athletes with two competition seasons: concentrate the strength means before each, rather than spreading them in one long wave. Inference: the design held running constant, so it isolates the strength distribution, which makes it a cleaner case than most in the chapter.

+**When NOT to apply** — The book gives no group sizes, athlete level, statistics or description of the strength means themselves. "Single-peak" and "double-peaked" describe the shape of the strength-means curve over the year; the timing of the single peak is not given. Inference: the result is in middle-distance runners with winter and summer seasons; it does not directly address a sport with one long competitive season such as college football.

+**Example** — The authors' own: Group 2 (strength means concentrated in December and March-April) improved 800 m by an average of 4.8 s and 1500 m by 6.3 s in the summer competition stage, against 3.4 s and 4.6 s for Group 1 (PDF p. 378).

+**Related** — [[claim--concentrated-beats-distributed-loading-for-highly-qualified-athletes]], [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]], [[framework--three-levels-of-change-in-fitness-state]], [[claim--middle-distance-runners-need-strength-and-jump-training-benchmarks]], [[claim--local-blood-flow-not-vo2max-tracks-competition-period-endurance-gains]] (also cites Sirenko), [[claim--endurance-rests-on-muscle-oxidative-and-strength-qualities-not-vo2max]]

3. "Long-term compensatory adaptation cannot continue indefinitely." Its effect "diminishes with each repetition," described "by a parabola whose peak is eventually reached with time (Fig 6.22, graph A). This indicates that an athlete's general adaptation reserves have a limit that is genetically predetermined." The limit shows as "waves in the dynamics of special work capacity (graphs B and C)," caused partly by "traditional periodisation" but "a more important reason is the exhaustion of the so-called current adaptation reserves (CAR) of the body."

Fig 6.13 is a scheme the authors say "need not be described in much detail," with no data (PDF p. 349 / printed p. 338).

**Example** — The authors' own: the VO2 max fall in the competition period, which puzzled specialists who studied only respiration but would have been expected by anyone also studying the working muscles (PDF p. 350 / printed p. 339).
